Sparse Predict and Demote:
Optimal Scheduling with Minimal Size Advice

Chengyi Liu ††thanks: California Institute of Technology, c.liu@caltech.edu    Thodoris Lykouris ††thanks: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, lykouris@mit.edu    Junxuan Shen ††thanks: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, junxuan@mit.edu    Adam Wierman ††thanks: California Institute of Technology, adamw@caltech.edu
Abstract

Knowledge of job sizes is crucial for optimizing the mean response time in single-server scheduling. However, predictions of job sizes are typically inexact and may be costly to obtain. Thus, a long-standing research question is: what is the minimal information about job sizes required to obtain near-optimal mean response time? We introduce a novel policy, Sparse Predict and Demote (SPD), and prove that it achieves order-optimal mean response time in heavy traffic while requiring only one-bit job-size predictions for a vanishing fraction of arrivals. SPD achieves heavy-traffic order-optimality even in situations when predictions are (i) inexact up to any fixed multiplicative error bound, and (ii) costly, i.e., the server is used to compute predictions and is thus unavailable to serve jobs while processing prediction queries. Finally, we use numerical experiments to illustrate that SPD maintains near-optimal performance beyond the heavy-traffic regime.

1 Introduction

A foundational result in scheduling theory is the optimality of Shortest Remaining Processing Time (SRPT) scheduling for a single-server queue [25, 26]. SRPT is optimal for the mean response time (i.e., sojourn time or flow time) in any single-server system, regardless of the arrival process or job size distribution (i.e., service distribution). Not only is SRPT optimal, but the reduction in mean response time that results from using size information to prioritize small jobs is an order of magnitude [16, 12]. For example, consider a single-server system with arrival rate λ\lambda, service rate μ\mu, and load ρ=λ/μ\rho=\lambda/\mu. In heavy traffic (ρ→1\rho\rightarrow 1), SRPT has mean response time Θ⁡(1/((1−ρ)​log⁡(1/(1−ρ)))CLOSE\Theta(1/((1-\rho)\log(1/(1-\rho))), which improves over the mean response time Θ⁡(1/(1−ρ))\Theta\left(1/(1-\rho)\right) of optimal size-oblivious algorithms. This contrast is not unique to exponential service distributions; it extends to a general class of distributions (see Section 2.1 for detailed discussion).

While SRPT is optimal, it is rarely used ‘as is’ in applications. In particular, schedulers typically do not have access to the exact sizes of jobs. Job sizes need to be estimated and, often, determining a job size estimate requires use of the server. For example, in the case of scheduling in compute systems, a server may use an AI model to estimate job sizes, which requires allocating the server to an inference task for some period of time during which it is unavailable to serve arriving jobs. Further, these estimates are not perfect; they arrive with prediction errors. These challenges are not unique to computer systems. Another example comes from emergency room resource allocation. Patient prioritization is informed by quick but error-prone initial screening that is performed by the same clinicians who treat patients. An automobile service center faces the same tradeoff. A mechanic must perform an initial shallow check to diagnose the problem and better schedule an incoming job, but the time spent on these checks comes at the expense of serving existing jobs.

Given the challenges associated with using SRPT in practice, it is not surprising that a long-standing direction for the field has been to understand how to (nearly) match the performance of SRPT while using less information about jobs. For example, previous work has sought to understand the impact of noisy predictions [33, 11, 10, 21, 27, 22], has studied the role of using a finite (small) set of priority classes instead of exact sizes for prioritization (e.g., classifying jobs as either small or large) [13, 24, 22, 7]; and recently the impact of using predictions of only a subset of the jobs has begun to receive attention [32]. However, while these lines of work provide specific policies that reduce the size information required by SRPT, the broad question of what is the minimal information that is needed to match the performance of SRPT remains open. In this work, we ask:

What is the minimal size information that enables order-optimal mean response time in heavy traffic?
How should scheduling policies adapt to predictions that are costly and/or inexact?

More specifically, our work both (i) introduces and analyzes policies that effectively use the minimal number of costly, inexact job-size estimates to attain order-optimal mean response time in heavy traffic, when achievable, and (ii) characterizes what size information is necessary to achieve order-optimal mean response time in heavy traffic. Further, we show how these results are impacted by the cost and error of size predictions.

1.1 Our results

We begin by focusing on the case where size predictions are both free and exact. In this setting, our first set of results (Section 3) establishes that binary size advice for each job suffices for order-optimal mean response time in heavy traffic in a general class of lognormal-or-lighter service distributions that includes the exponential service distribution. In particular, we introduce the Predict and Demote policy that operates a high-priority and a low-priority queue as follows. Upon arrival of a job, the advice communicates whether the job size is above a carefully selected size threshold; this size advice is binary (and thus minimal) for each job. If jobs are present in both queues, the high-priority queue is always prioritized. Within each queue, we prioritize jobs in increasing order of their arrival, i.e., based on First Come First Served (FCFS). Surprisingly, this simple algorithm attains order-optimal mean response time in heavy traffic (Theorem 3.5). We complement this result by showing that for a class of distributions outside this family, no assignment of jobs to two FCFS priority queues using binary size advice attains the SRPT order (Theorem 3.8). The latter result shows that binary size advice does not always recover the improvements of full size information.

Our second set of results (Section 4) builds on the first to show that binary predictions are not needed for every job; rather, the aforementioned improvements only require advice for a vanishing fraction of incoming jobs. In particular, we introduce the Sparse Predict and Demote (SPD) policy, which obtains binary size advice for a sparse selection of jobs and demotes to the low-priority queue any queried job that has remaining size greater than a carefully chosen size threshold that we refer to as the residual demotion barrier. The simplest way to attain the sparse set is by querying any arriving job with a vanishingly small probability. We show that SPD achieves an order-optimal mean response time in heavy traffic for any lognormal-or-lighter service distribution with such sparse predictions at arrival (Theorem 4.3). That said, the same guarantee can also be attained when the algorithm queries jobs only if it has not finished after a particular amount of service that is carefully selected such that a vanishing fraction of jobs end up being queried (Theorem 4.6).

We next address the question of what happens outside of the lognormal-or-lighter family of distributions (Section 4.3). We show that SPD can attain heavy-traffic order-optimality for a class of service distributions outside this family by obtaining exact sizes for a vanishing fraction of jobs and using SRPT in the low-priority queue (Theorem 4.7). In particular, knowing the remaining sizes of demoted jobs lets shorter jobs bypass larger ones in this queue. This controls the delay of a larger demoted population, allowing us to remove enough work from high priority to attain the SRPT order while still querying a vanishing fraction of arrivals.

Our final analytic result is for the setting where size advice comes at a cost and is inexact (Section 5). Here, we show how the design of SPD must adapt to these challenges. In particular, for a given error parameter ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), we allow the size advice to be any number within a (1±ε)(1\pm\varepsilon) multiplicative interval of the true size (possibly adversarially selected). We also assume that a size query for a specific job requires some inference duration during which the server is occupied and cannot serve any job. As long as the inference duration asymptotically decays as a power function of the system slack 1−ρ1-\rho, we establish that SPD remains heavy-traffic order-optimal for lognormal-or-lighter service distributions under such costly and inexact size advice (Theorem 5.7). Interestingly, in the presence of costs, the two sparsity mechanisms (query with some probability at arrival and query upon receiving some amount of service) are not interchangeable: heavy-traffic optimality requires carefully tuning these two mechanisms to the service distribution (Proposition 5.4).

Our analytic results focus exclusively on heavy-traffic performance. We conclude the paper with numerical evaluations that establish that SPD performs well outside of the heavy-traffic regime too (Section 6). These experiments highlight that the design insights that lead to SPD are useful beyond heavy-traffic.

1.2 Our techniques

To demonstrate our technical contributions, we use exponential service distributions as an illustrative example. Recall that the optimal scheduling algorithm (SRPT) has mean response time that scales as Θ⁡(1/((1−ρ)​log⁡(1/(1−ρ)))CLOSE\Theta(1/((1-\rho)\log(1/(1-\rho))) in this setting, where 1−ρ1-\rho is the system slack. In contrast, FCFS enjoys the optimal size-oblivious mean response time of Θ⁡(1/(1−ρ))\Theta\left(1/(1-\rho)\right).

The key to attaining the SRPT order with sparse binary advice is to balance the system slack of the high-priority queue with the fraction of jobs that are demoted to the low-priority queue. By demoting jobs with sufficiently large remaining size (via an appropriate residual demotion barrier), we remove sufficient load from the high-priority queue. This increases its system slack to 1−ρHIGH=Θ⁡((1−ρ)​log⁡(1/(1−ρ)))1-\rho^{\textsc{HIGH}}=\Theta((1-\rho)\log\left(1/(1-\rho)\right)), which enables FCFS to attain the optimal size-aware mean response time on this queue. That said, if we demote too many jobs, the low-priority queue may end up suffering. To circumvent this, the selection of the residual barrier together with the sparsity mechanism is done in a way that only a O⁡(1−ρ)O(1-\rho) fraction of jobs is demoted; this controls the contribution of demoted jobs to the overall mean response time. Interestingly, we can show that a queried job has remaining size greater than the selected residual demotion barrier with probability ω⁡(1−ρ)\omega(1-\rho) (see Lemma 4.2). Hence, querying a vanishingly small fraction of jobs suffices to ensure that 1−ρ1-\rho fraction of jobs are demoted.

Moving to costly and inexact predictions, we need a more refined approach towards the sparsity mechanism. In the presence of costs, predictions introduce additional load to the system. To maintain the optimality guarantees, the sparsity mechanism should be selected in a way that ensures that this additional load is at most a constant fraction of the original system slack. This is only achievable if the cost from the minimum number of queries that are needed to ensure sufficient demotion of jobs to the low-priority queue is controllable. As a result, for a given cost per query, the optimal sparsity mechanism needs to minimize the self-information, the negative logarithm of the probability that a queried job qualifies for demotion under exact predictions. We show that, for our results to extend to costly predictions, this self-information must be small enough to preserve a fixed fraction of the slack after accounting for inference costs (Lemma 5.3). This result provides a toolbox towards handling inexact predictions. In particular, we create a finite collection of candidate sparsity mechanisms whose size depends only on the inference-cost exponent and show that their self-information values sum to at most −log⁡(1−ρ)-\log(1-\rho), so at least one mechanism has inference load negligible relative to the original slack (Lemma 5.6), thereby asymptotically preserving the original system slack despite the additional inference load.

1.3 Related work

Our work contributes to two distinct literatures: (i) the study of size-aware scheduling in queueing systems and (ii) the study of online algorithms with advice (a.k.a. learning-augmented online algorithms). We discuss each in turn.

Size-aware scheduling. The field of scheduling in single-server queueing systems is classical. Priority-based policies, including size-based and age-based policies, have well-known closed-form characterizations; e.g., see [13, 15]. In fact, recent work has provided an analysis of a very broad class of priority-based policies, beyond the classically studied policies, via the SOAP classification (see Section 2.2) [28]. SRPT has been known to be optimal for mean response time for decades, since [25, 26] and has received considerable attention as a result. Most relevant to the current work is analysis of its heavy traffic behavior [16, 12, 3]. However, the task of understanding the minimal amount of size information necessary to be nearly optimal remains unanswered and has received considerable attention in recent years. In particular, while classic results focus on situations where policies are either size-aware or size-oblivious, e.g., [29, 23, 31], recently work has begun to focus on situations where exact sizes are not known, but approximate sizes are used for prioritization [33, 11, 10, 21, 27, 22]. A traditional approach for system design using prioritization is the multilevel queue (MLQ) policy, which adjusts priorities as jobs receive service without requiring advance knowledge of their processing times [8, 5]. Recent work has increasingly studied policies that place jobs into a finite set of priority classes, typically based on size, as a way to minimize the amount of size information that needs to be predicted. Such policies have a long history, e.g., see [15, 13, 24] and the references therein, and have received renewed attention in recent years motivated by the goal of scheduling with minimal size information [22, 7, 30]. Additionally, motivated by predictions via costly AI inferences, very recent work has focused on the goal of reducing the number of jobs for which size predictions are requested [32, 19].

From the literature reviewed above, the most related papers to our work are those that focus on the design of algorithms that use limited size information to provide performance that is robust to costly and/or inexact predictions. In particular, [27] shows that a simple scheduling policy can achieve near-optimal performance with accurate estimates while remaining robust to prediction errors. Building on this, more recent work in [32] introduces algorithms that selectively request predictions, outperforming those that predict every job. The DelayPredict policy presented in this work serves as a baseline in our experimental results and is a special case of the SPD policy we introduce in this paper. Finally, the most related work to the current paper is [22, 7], which both study the performance of policies that use one-bit predictions in order to place jobs into two priority queues. [22] has a different focus than the current paper. It uses mean-field analysis to study a multi-server system. On the other hand, [7] studies the heavy-traffic behavior of a single server with two priority queues facing general arrival and service rates. The results of [7] are similar in spirit to our warmup results in Section 3.1. They show that, by categorizing jobs as either large or small, it is possible to asymptotically recover the mean response time of SRPT in heavy traffic. Although this result is qualitatively similar to Theorem 3.5 of our paper, the results are not directly comparable. [7] considers more general arrival distribution patterns, which prevents the derivation and use of explicit characterizations of the mean response time as a function of load. Moreover, their result is restricted to a special case of service distributions. In contrast, we provide a full characterization across all service distributions, showing when a two-class policy (a.k.a. one-bit predictions) is, and is not, enough. Further, there is no parallel in [7] for our results on the use of a vanishing fraction of predictions or the consideration of costly or inexact predictions.

Online algorithms with advice. The field of online algorithms with (machine-learned) advice is a relatively new area, which emerged following the work of [18]. Since then, a wide range of online problems have been explored wthin this framework; a recent survey of this field can be found in [20] and an online repository of related work is available at [17]. Within the broad area of scheduling and resource allocation, a number of problems have been studied, including quantifying prediction error costs [21], designing robust policies under misprediction [27], and load-balancing of large databases [1]. Notably, the key assumption in nearly all of this work is that predictions are provided at no cost. An exception to this is the literature on online learning with hints [6, 9] and parsimonious learning-augmented online algorithms [14, 2], where the economic cost associated with predictions is considered. However, the question of how to manage the interference of computational resources in algorithms with machine-learned advice has not been explored. Our work presents results addressing this interference in the context of online scheduling.

2 Model and Preliminaries

We study the M/GI/1 queueing model in heavy traffic. In this model, jobs arrive at a unit-speed single server as a Poisson process of rate λρ\lambda_{\rho}. Their sizes S∼FS\sim F are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables drawn from a service distribution FF and independent of the arrival process. With mean job size 𝔼⁡[S]\mathbb{E}[S], the unit-speed server has service rate μ:=1/𝔼⁡[S]\mu:=1/{\mathbb{E}[S]}. We assume that (in the absence of inference work) the system is stable, that is, the arrival rate is smaller than the service rate. As a result, λρ:=ρ​μ\lambda_{\rho}:=\rho\mu for some ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1), where ρ=λρ​𝔼​[S]\rho=\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[S] is the ordinary-service load, and 1−ρ1-\rho is the ordinary-service slack, the fraction of server capacity left after ordinary service, before inference work is added. A scheduling policy π\pi decides which job receives service and when to request a prediction; service may be preempted and resumed without repeating previously completed service. In a stable system, a policy π\pi induces a steady-state response time TπT^{\pi}, the time from arrival to completion of a typical job. Our objective is to minimize its mean 𝔼⁡[Tπ]\mathbb{E}[T^{\pi}].

We study the heavy-traffic limit ρ↑1\rho\uparrow 1, equivalently λρ↑μ\lambda_{\rho}\uparrow\mu, with the service distribution fixed. As the ordinary-service slack 1−ρ1-\rho vanishes, we compare the rates at which mean response times diverge under different scheduling policies. When the load is fixed, we suppress its subscript and write λ\lambda. To state the relevant heavy-traffic benchmarks, we define the workload distribution

G⁡(x):=𝔼[S𝟏{S≤x}]𝔼⁡[S],G(x):=\frac{\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{S\leq x\}]}{\mathbb{E}[S]}, (1)

which is the fraction of the workload contributed by jobs of size at most xx. Hence, G−1​(ρ)G^{-1}(\rho) is the size cutoff above which jobs contribute exactly a 1−ρ1-\rho fraction of the total workload: 𝔼[S𝟏{S>G−1(ρ)}]=(1−ρ)𝔼[S]\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{S>G^{-1}(\rho)\}]=(1-\rho)\mathbb{E}[S].

Shortest Remaining Processing Time (SRPT) always serves the job with the smallest true remaining size. Under Assumption 1 on the job size distribution (see Section 2.1), the heavy-traffic characterization of [16] gives that the optimal size-aware mean response time, attained by SRPT:

𝔼⁡[TSRPT]=Θ⁡(1(1−ρ)​G−1​(ρ)).\mathbb{E}\left[T^{\mathrm{SRPT}}\right]=\Theta\!\left(\frac{1}{(1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho)}\right). (2)

Since the service distribution has unbounded support, G−1​(ρ)→∞G^{-1}(\rho)\to\infty as ρ↑1\rho\uparrow 1. We call a policy heavy-traffic order-optimal if its mean response time is within a constant factor of this benchmark as ρ↑1\rho\uparrow 1. Our goal is to design heavy-traffic order-optimal policies when only given access to inexact and costly size predictions for only a small fraction of jobs. We first assume predictions are exact and free (Sections 3 and 4). We then allow predictions to require inference work on the same server competing with job service (Section 5.1), and be inexact (Section 5.2).

2.1 Classes of Service Distributions

The relevance of job-size information depends strongly on the service-time tail. Let ff denote the density of FF, and write F¯​(x):=ℙ​(S>x)\overline{F}(x):=\mathbb{P}(S>x). The hazard rate h​(x):=f​(x)/F¯​(x)h(x):={f(x)}/{\overline{F}(x)} is the instantaneous completion rate at size xx, conditional on the job requiring at least xx units of service. For ease of exposition, we restrict attention to distributions with unbounded support and with continuous, strictly positive hazard rate for x>0x>0. We organize service distributions according to the asymptotic growth of their cumulative hazard

H⁡(x):=∫0xh⁡(t)​𝑑t=−log⁡F¯​(x);H(x):=\int_{0}^{x}h(t)\,dt=-\log\overline{F}(x);

faster growth of HH means faster decay of the service-time tail.

Our main focus is the lognormal-or-lighter regime, which begins at H⁡(x)=Θ⁡((log⁡x)2)H(x)=\Theta((\log x)^{2}) and contains all faster-growing cumulative hazards. This regime contains many classical service distributions. Lognormal-type tails lie at the boundary, with H⁡(x)∼A​(log⁡x)2H(x)\sim A(\log x)^{2} for A>0A>0. Weibull tails have H⁡(x)=(x/c)νH(x)=(x/c)^{\nu} for c,ν>0c,\nu>0, which grows faster than (log⁡x)2(\log x)^{2}; the exponential distribution is the classical Weibull case ν=1\nu=1. Doubly exponential tails provide another example: H⁡(x)=ec​x−1H(x)=e^{cx}-1 with c>0c>0 growing faster than every power of xx. To place them in context, letting f⁡(x)≪g⁡(x)f(x)\ll g(x) denote f⁡(x)=o⁡(g⁡(x))f(x)=o(g(x)), we distinguish three tail regimes:11 1 Since F¯​(x)=e−H⁡(x)\overline{F}(x)=e^{-H(x)}, larger values of H⁡(x)H(x) mean smaller tail probabilities. Faster growth of HH therefore corresponds to a lighter service-time tail.

H⁡(x)=Ω⁡((log⁡x)2)⏟lognormal-or-lighter|log⁡x≪H⁡(x)≪(log⁡x)2⏟intermediate|H⁡(x)=O⁡(log⁡x)⏟Pareto-or-heavier,\underbrace{H(x)=\Omega\!\left((\log x)^{2}\right)}_{\text{lognormal-or-lighter}}\qquad\Big|\qquad\underbrace{\log x\ll H(x)\ll(\log x)^{2}}_{\text{intermediate}}\qquad\Big|\qquad\underbrace{H(x)=O(\log x)}_{\text{Pareto-or-heavier}},

The intermediate regime consists of tails that decay faster than every power law but remain heavier than the boundary of the lognormal-or-lighter regime; for example, H⁡(x)∼(log⁡x)rH(x)\sim(\log x)^{r} with 1<r<21<r<2.

The Pareto-or-heavier regime contains Pareto and other power-law-type tails: H⁡(x)=O⁡(log⁡x)H(x)=O(\log x) implies that F¯​(x)≥x−C\overline{F}(x)\geq x^{-C} for some C<∞C<\infty and all sufficiently large xx. For such distributions, it is known that size-oblivious policies can maintain heavy-traffic order-optimality. For example, for Pareto service distributions with finite variance, the size-unaware Foreground–Background (FB) policy, which prioritizes jobs with the least attained service, is known to achieve the same heavy-traffic order as size-aware SRPT [23, 4]. This motivates our focus on the intermediate and lognormal-or-lighter regimes.

Assumption 1 states the conditions on the service distribution that are assumed throughout the paper. Note that we omit it from individual result statements to avoid repetition.

2.2 Brief Overview of the SOAP Framework

In our analysis, we repeatedly apply the SOAP framework [28] to derive response times of SPD and its variations. In this framework, a job is described by its age aa, the total service it has received, including inference work when a costly prediction is requested, together with a descriptor dd recording job-specific information such as a prediction or whether the job is selected for a query. SOAP then assigns the job a rank r⁡(d,a)r(d,a), with smaller rank corresponding to higher priority, and always serves the job with smallest rank, breaking ties in favor of the job that arrived first (first-come, first-served, or FCFS). For delayed predictions, the rank function simply does not use the prediction until the age at which it becomes available.33 3 Equivalently, for the purpose of the SOAP representation, the descriptor may encode the eventual prediction outcome, while the rank function ignores that component before the prediction is activated. In the SOAP formulas, xx denotes a tagged job’s total server work; it equals its ordinary size when predictions are free and includes inference work otherwise. For a tagged job with descriptor dd and total work xx, let Td,xT_{d,x} denote its response time. This is the sum of its waiting time, from arrival until it first receives service, and its residence time, from first service until completion, including any interruptions.

We first consider the simpler case in which a⟼r⁡(d,a)a\longmapsto r(d,a) is non-increasing for every descriptor dd. In this case, a job’s priority can only improve as it receives service; this is indeed the case for several canonical policies including SRPT and fixed-rank priority policies. To describe the response time of a tagged job, fix a rank rr. With FCFS tie-breaking, an older job wins an equal-rank tie. Service is relevant to rank rr if it can be served ahead of a tagged job of rank rr. Thus old-job service is relevant to ranks at most rr, while new-job service is relevant only to ranks strictly below rr. Let Xnew​[r]X^{\mathrm{new}}[r] denote the total server work of a newly arriving job if its initial rank is strictly below rr, and zero otherwise; a non-increasing rank remains below rr once it starts there. For jobs that arrived before the tagged job, SOAP similarly distinguishes relevant service according to whether the job is relevant from its arrival or becomes relevant only after receiving some service. We denote the corresponding amounts of service by X0old​[r]X_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[r] and X1old​[r]X_{1}^{\mathrm{old}}[r], respectively. When ranks are non-increasing, a job can cross the threshold rr at most once, so there are no further relevant intervals. Define ρnew​[r]:=λ​𝔼​[Xnew​[r]]\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[r]:=\lambda\mathbb{E}[X^{\mathrm{new}}[r]] and ρ0old​[r]:=λ​𝔼​[X0old​[r]]\rho_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[r]:=\lambda\mathbb{E}[X_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[r]].

Proposition 2.1 (Non-increasing-rank case of SOAP [28, Theorem 5.5]).

Suppose that a↦r⁡(d,a)a\mapsto r(d,a) is non-increasing for every descriptor dd. Then the conditional mean response time of a job with descriptor dd and total work xx is

𝔼⁡[Td,x]=λ⁡(𝔼⁡[(X0old​[r⁡(d,0)])2]+𝔼⁡[(X1old​[r⁡(d,0)])2])2​(1−ρ0old​[r⁡(d,0)])​(1−ρnew​[r⁡(d,0)])⏟expected waiting time+∫0xd​a1−ρnew​[r⁡(d,a)]⏟expected residence time.\mathbb{E}[T_{d,x}]=\underbrace{\frac{\lambda\left(\mathbb{E}\!\left[(X_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[r(d,0)])^{2}\right]+\mathbb{E}\!\left[(X_{1}^{\mathrm{old}}[r(d,0)])^{2}\right]\right)}{2\left(1-\rho_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[r(d,0)]\right)\left(1-\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[r(d,0)]\right)}}_{\text{expected waiting time}}+\underbrace{\int_{0}^{x}\frac{da}{1-\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[r(d,a)]}}_{\text{expected residence time}}.

To interpret this formula, note that in the waiting-time denominator, 1−ρ0old​[r]1-\rho_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[r] measures the slack against relevant work already present when the tagged job arrives, while 1−ρnew​[r]1-\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[r] measures the slack against relevant work generated by future arrivals. The residence term accumulates the reciprocal of this latter slack as the tagged job progresses through its rank trajectory. For example, with no inference work, FCFS has ρ0old=ρ\rho_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}=\rho and ρnew=0\rho^{\mathrm{new}}=0, so the vanishing slack in the waiting-time denominator gives 𝔼⁡[TFCFS]=Θ⁡(1/(1−ρ))\mathbb{E}[T^{\mathrm{FCFS}}]=\Theta(1/(1-\rho)), a factor of order G−1​(ρ)G^{-1}(\rho) above SRPT. Details of this calculation are given in Appendix B.1.

A similar response-time formula holds even when ranks increase at some ages; Appendix B.2 gives this more general result in Proposition B.2 and its intuition. The proof of Proposition 2.1 follows directly from this more general proposition by specializing to non-increasing ranks.

3 The Power and Limits of Binary-Level Queues

A multilevel queue (MLQ) scheduler organizes jobs into a finite set of priority queues. Scheduling then involves two decisions: which queue receives service and which job is served within that queue. In the strict preemptive-priority version considered here, the server always works on the highest-priority nonempty queue; a job in a lower-priority queue is interrupted whenever higher-priority work becomes available. A separate rule, such as FCFS, determines the service order within each queue. Assigning jobs to queues therefore allows the scheduler to favor some jobs without maintaining a complete ordering of all jobs by size.

In this section, we study the simplest such system: binary-level queues (BLQ), with just a high-priority queue and a low-priority queue, both served according to FCFS. For each load ρ\rho, every arriving job receives a size prediction, which the scheduler uses to assign a binary rank Rρ∈{0,1}R_{\rho}\in\{0,1\}. Ranks 00 and 11 designate the high-priority and low-priority queues, respectively. Each job keeps this rank until completion. Thus, the prediction is used only for the initial queue assignment: afterward, the scheduler retains one bit per job (its rank) and uses FCFS within each queue.

Formally, a BLQ policy is specified by a measurable assignment map φρ:ℝ+→[0,1]\varphi_{\rho}:\mathbb{R}_{+}\to[0,1], where ℙ⁡(Rρ=1∣S=s)=φρ​(s)\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}=1\mid S=s)=\varphi_{\rho}(s). Thus, φρ​(s)\varphi_{\rho}(s) is the probability of assigning low priority to a job of size ss. Values in {0,1}\{0,1\} give deterministic size partitions; values in (0,1)(0,1) allow randomization, independent across arrivals and of the queue state conditional on job sizes. We also use φρ\varphi_{\rho} to denote the induced BLQ policy. The high-priority load and slack are ρHIGH:=λρ𝔼[S𝟏{Rρ=0}]\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}:=\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=0\}] and 1−ρHIGH=(1−ρ)+λρ𝔼[S𝟏{Rρ=1}]1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}=(1-\rho)+\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=1\}] respectively. Note that assigning work to the low-priority queue creates additional slack for the high-priority queue. Since ranks remain fixed (and are thus non-increasing), Proposition 2.1 applies. The next two lemmas give the response-time contribution of each queue and follow from standard arguments [15, 13]. We provide their proof for completeness in Appendix C.1 and a proof sketch below.

Lemma 3.1 (Response time of the high-priority queue).

Under any BLQ policy φρ\varphi_{\rho}, the contribution of the high-priority queue to the overall mean response time is

𝔼[Tφρ𝟏{Rρ=0}]=ℙ(Rρ=0)λρ𝔼[S2𝟏{Rρ=0}]2​(1−ρHIGH)+𝔼[S𝟏{Rρ=0}].\mathbb{E}\!\left[T^{\varphi_{\rho}}\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=0\}\right]=\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}=0)\frac{\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}\!\left[S^{2}\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=0\}\right]}{2(1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}})}+\mathbb{E}\!\left[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=0\}\right].
Lemma 3.2 (Response time of the low-priority queue).

Under any BLQ policy φρ\varphi_{\rho}, the contribution of the low-priority queue to the overall mean response time is

𝔼[Tφρ𝟏{Rρ=1}]=ℙ(Rρ=1)λρ​𝔼​[S2]2​(1−ρ)​(1−ρHIGH)+𝔼[S𝟏{Rρ=1}]1−ρHIGH.\mathbb{E}\!\left[T^{\varphi_{\rho}}\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=1\}\right]=\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}=1)\frac{\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[S^{2}]}{2(1-\rho)(1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}})}+\frac{\mathbb{E}\!\left[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=1\}\right]}{1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}}.
Proof sketch of Lemmas 3.1 and 3.2.

Both identities follow from Proposition 2.1. A high-priority tagged job waits only for older high-priority work; FCFS keeps future arrivals behind it. A low-priority tagged job waits for all older work and can be overtaken only by future high-priority arrivals. High-priority residence is uninterrupted, whereas high-priority interruptions stretch low-priority residence by the reciprocal high-priority slack. Substituting these quantities and averaging over each rank gives the identities. ∎

These two lemmas show how the queue assignment affects mean response time. Routing a job to the low-priority queue removes its size from the load that can delay high-priority jobs. However, the demoted job must now wait for high-priority work as well. Its longer delay is weighted by the probability of demotion in the overall mean. Selecting large jobs for demotion can therefore reduce the high-priority load substantially while making only a small fraction of arrivals incur low-priority delay. We next choose a size cutoff that balances the work removed from high priority against the fraction of arrivals sent to low priority.

3.1 When Does One Free Bit Suffice?

We begin by showing that a simple BLQ policy suffices to obtain heavy-traffic order-optimal mean response time. In particular, our warm-up policy, Predict and Demote, PD(bb), uses a residual demotion barrier b≥0b\geq 0, predicting at the arrival of every job whether its remaining size exceeds bb. Since the job has received no service at arrival, its remaining size is exactly SS, giving Rρ=𝟏{S>b}R_{\rho}=\mathbf{1}\{S>b\}. The comparison is made once, so a demoted job stays in the low-priority queue through completion.

To choose bb, we first consider how often jobs should be demoted. In Lemma 3.2, the low-priority waiting contribution contains the factor ℙ⁡(Rρ=1)/(1−ρ)\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}=1)/(1-\rho). Setting the demotion probability to 1−ρ1-\rho makes this factor equal to one: the small fraction of demoted jobs offsets the additional waiting factor 1/(1−ρ)1/(1-\rho) they experience. Both queues’ waiting contributions can then be bounded on the scale 1/(1−ρHIGH)1/(1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}). Among all assignments with demotion probability 1−ρ1-\rho, choosing the largest jobs removes the most expected service per arrival from the high-priority queue. This motivates the slack-matched size cutoff

s¯ρ=F¯−1​(1−ρ).\bar{s}_{\rho}=\overline{F}^{-1}(1-\rho). (3)

Under PD⁡(s¯ρ)\mathrm{PD}(\bar{s}_{\rho}), this cutoff selects the largest 1−ρ1-\rho fraction of arrivals for the low-priority queue. The next lemma states this demotion probability, which we use to bound the low-priority queue’s contribution to the mean response time. Its proof follows directly as ℙ⁡(Rρ=1)=F¯​(s¯ρ)=1−ρ\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}=1)=\overline{F}(\bar{s}_{\rho})=1-\rho.

Lemma 3.3 (Low-priority fraction at s¯ρ\bar{s}_{\rho}).

Under PD⁡(s¯ρ)\mathrm{PD}(\bar{s}_{\rho}), ℙ⁡(Rρ=1)=1−ρ\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}=1)=1-\rho.

This demotion probability determines the fraction of arrivals that incur low-priority delay. We must also show that their demotion removes enough work from the high-priority queue. Every demoted job has more than s¯ρ\bar{s}_{\rho} service remaining, so together they remove at least (1−ρ)​s¯ρ(1-\rho)\bar{s}_{\rho} service per arrival from that queue. In the lognormal-or-lighter regime, the next lemma (proof in Appendix C.2) shows that s¯ρ\bar{s}_{\rho} is on the G−1​(ρ)G^{-1}(\rho) scale. The resulting high-priority slack is therefore at least of order (1−ρ)​G−1​(ρ)(1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho), which makes the waiting-time bound match the SRPT benchmark.

Lemma 3.4 (Asymptotic scale of s¯ρ\bar{s}_{\rho}).

For distributions in the lognormal-or-lighter regime, there exists a constant θ¯∈(0,1]\bar{\theta}\in(0,1] such that the slack-matched size cutoff satisfies s¯ρG−1​(ρ)⟶θ¯\frac{\bar{s}_{\rho}}{G^{-1}(\rho)}\longrightarrow\bar{\theta}.

Theorem 3.5 (One free bit suffices in the lognormal-or-lighter regime).

For distributions in the lognormal-or-lighter regime, PD⁡(s¯ρ)\mathrm{PD}(\bar{s}_{\rho}) is heavy-traffic order-optimal, i.e., 𝔼⁡[TPD⁡(s¯ρ)]=Θ⁡(𝔼⁡[TSRPT])\mathbb{E}[T^{\mathrm{PD}(\bar{s}_{\rho})}]=\Theta\!\left(\mathbb{E}[T^{\mathrm{SRPT}}]\right).

Proof.

By Lemmas 3.3 and 3.4, ℙ⁡(Rρ=1)=1−ρ\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}=1)=1-\rho and s¯ρ=Θ⁡(G−1​(ρ))\bar{s}_{\rho}=\Theta(G^{-1}(\rho)). Since each demoted job has size greater than s¯ρ\bar{s}_{\rho}, the high-priority slack satisfies

1−ρHIGH≥λρ​s¯ρ​(1−ρ)=Ω⁡((1−ρ)​G−1​(ρ)).1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}\geq\lambda_{\rho}\bar{s}_{\rho}(1-\rho)=\Omega\!\left((1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho)\right). (4)

For the waiting contributions, Lemmas 3.1 and 3.2 give the following bounds for the high-priority and low-priority queues, respectively:

ℙ⁡(Rρ=0)​λρ𝔼[S2𝟏{Rρ=0}]2​(1−ρHIGH)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}=0)\frac{\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[S^{2}\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=0\}]}{2(1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}})} ≤λρ​𝔼​[S2]2​(1−ρHIGH),\displaystyle\leq\frac{\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[S^{2}]}{2(1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}})},
ℙ⁡(Rρ=1)​λρ​𝔼​[S2]2​(1−ρ)​(1−ρHIGH)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}=1)\frac{\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[S^{2}]}{2(1-\rho)(1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}})} =(1−ρ)​λρ​𝔼​[S2]2​(1−ρ)​(1−ρHIGH)=λρ​𝔼​[S2]2​(1−ρHIGH).\displaystyle=\frac{(1-\rho)\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[S^{2}]}{2(1-\rho)(1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}})}=\frac{\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[S^{2}]}{2(1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}})}.

In the second calculation, Lemma 3.3 lets us replace ℙ⁡(Rρ=1)\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}=1) by 1−ρ1-\rho, which cancels the same factor in the denominator. The residence contributions are at most 𝔼⁡[S]\mathbb{E}[S] and 1/λρ1/\lambda_{\rho}, respectively; the latter follows from 1−ρHIGH=(1−ρ)+λρ𝔼[S𝟏{Rρ=1}]≥λρ𝔼[S𝟏{Rρ=1}]1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}=(1-\rho)+\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=1\}]\geq\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=1\}].
