where we used (4), 𝔼⁡[S2]<∞\mathbb{E}[S^{2}]<\infty, and λρ=Θ⁡(1)\lambda_{\rho}=\Theta(1). Finally, SRPT optimality gives 𝔼⁡[TPD⁡(s¯ρ)]≥𝔼⁡[TSRPT]\mathbb{E}[T^{\mathrm{PD}(\bar{s}_{\rho})}]\geq\mathbb{E}[T^{\mathrm{SRPT}}]; the SRPT mean response time in (2) supplies the matching lower bound. ∎

3.2 When Does One Free Bit Not Suffice?

In the previous section, we determined a class of distributions for which one free bit suffices under PD(bb); we now focus on the opposite. In particular, in this section we show that for service distributions in the intermediate regime of Section 2.1, no BLQ policy is heavy-traffic order-optimal. This statement holds for every measurable assignment map φρ:ℝ+→[0,1]\varphi_{\rho}:\mathbb{R}_{+}\to[0,1], even when the map is chosen based on the load ρ\rho.

An order-optimal policy must satisfy two requirements, formalized in Lemma 3.6 (proved in Appendix C.4). First, it must demote enough work to give the high-priority queue sufficient slack. Second, it must demote sufficiently few jobs to control the low-priority contribution to the overall mean response time. Together, these requirements force the average size of demoted jobs to be at least of order G−1​(ρ)G^{-1}(\rho).

Lemma 3.6 (Necessary size scale of the low-priority queue).

Suppose a BLQ policy φρ\varphi_{\rho} is heavy-traffic order-optimal along some sequence ρ↑1\rho\uparrow 1. Along that sequence,

𝔼[S𝟏{Rρ=1}]=Ω((1−ρ)G−1(ρ))and𝔼[S∣Rρ=1]=Ω(G−1(ρ)).\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=1\}]=\Omega\!\left((1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho)\right)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{E}[S\mid R_{\rho}=1]=\Omega\!\left(G^{-1}(\rho)\right).

In the intermediate regime, even all jobs above any fixed positive multiple of G−1​(ρ)G^{-1}(\rho) carry o⁡((1−ρ)​G−1​(ρ))o\!\left((1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho)\right) work per arrival. The next lemma establishes this scarcity bound (proof in Appendix C.5); combined with the average-size requirement, this prevents a BLQ policy from demoting enough work to obtain optimality.

Lemma 3.7 (Insufficient tail work in the intermediate regime).

For distributions in the intermediate regime, under Assumption 1, for every fixed d>0d>0, 𝔼[S𝟏{S>dG−1(ρ)}]=o((1−ρ)G−1(ρ))\mathbb{E}\!\left[S\mathbf{1}\{S>dG^{-1}(\rho)\}\right]=o\!\left((1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho)\right).

Combining Lemmas 3.6 and 3.7 gives the following impossibility result.

Theorem 3.8 (BLQ impossibility in the intermediate regime).

For distributions in the intermediate regime, every BLQ policy φρ\varphi_{\rho} is not heavy-traffic order-optimal, i.e.,

𝔼⁡[Tφρ]=ω⁡(1(1−ρ)​G−1​(ρ)).\mathbb{E}[T^{\varphi_{\rho}}]=\omega\!\left(\frac{1}{(1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho)}\right).
Proof of Theorem 3.8.

If the claimed ω\omega bound failed, there would be a sequence ρ↑1\rho\uparrow 1 along which 𝔼⁡[Tφρ]=O⁡(1/((1−ρ)​G−1​(ρ)))\mathbb{E}[T^{\varphi_{\rho}}]=O(1/((1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho))). Lemma 3.6 gives constants c0,c1>0c_{0},c_{1}>0 such that, eventually along the same sequence,

𝔼[S∣Rρ=1]≥c0G−1(ρ)and𝔼[S𝟏{Rρ=1}]≥c1(1−ρ)G−1(ρ).\mathbb{E}[S\mid R_{\rho}=1]\geq c_{0}G^{-1}(\rho)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=1\}]\geq c_{1}(1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho).

First consider the demoted jobs whose size is at most (c0/2)​G−1​(ρ)(c_{0}/2)G^{-1}(\rho). Their work per arrival is at most this size threshold times the probability of demotion. Hence

𝔼⁡[S​𝟏​{Rρ=1,S≤(c0/2)​G−1​(ρ)}]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=1,\ S\leq(c_{0}/2)G^{-1}(\rho)\}] ≤c02G−1(ρ)ℙ(Rρ=1)≤12𝔼[S𝟏{Rρ=1}].\displaystyle\leq\frac{c_{0}}{2}G^{-1}(\rho)\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}=1)\leq\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=1\}].

The second inequality follows from the average-size bound: multiplying 𝔼⁡[S∣Rρ=1]≥c0​G−1​(ρ)\mathbb{E}[S\mid R_{\rho}=1]\geq c_{0}G^{-1}(\rho) by ℙ⁡(Rρ=1)\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}=1) gives 𝔼[S𝟏{Rρ=1}]≥c0G−1(ρ)ℙ(Rρ=1)\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=1\}]\geq c_{0}G^{-1}(\rho)\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}=1). Thus demoted jobs at or below the threshold account for at most half of the demoted work, so demoted jobs above it account for at least half. The first expectation below counts the work of all jobs above the threshold, in either queue. The second counts only the demoted jobs above it. Since these are a subset of all jobs above the threshold and S≥0S\geq 0, we obtain

𝔼[S𝟏{S>(c0/2)G−1(ρ)}]≥𝔼[S𝟏{Rρ=1,S>(c0/2)G−1(ρ)}]≥12𝔼[S𝟏{Rρ=1}]≥c12(1−ρ)G−1(ρ).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{S>(c_{0}/2)G^{-1}(\rho)\}]\geq\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=1,\ S>(c_{0}/2)G^{-1}(\rho)\}]\geq\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=1\}]\geq\frac{c_{1}}{2}(1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho).

The last inequality uses the lower bound on total demoted work. This contradicts Lemma 3.7 with d=c0/2d=c_{0}/2. ∎

4 Sparse Predict & Demote: A Vanishing Prediction Rate Suffices

The previous section highlights that a scheduler can be heavy-traffic order-optimal using only one bit of information per job when the job size distribution is lognormal-or-lighter. Here, we show that one can use even less job size information while maintaining heavy-traffic order-optimal mean response times. Specifically, we ask if one bit is needed for every job or if a policy can still maintain heavy-traffic order-optimality without querying size predictions from every job.

To answer this question, we introduce a new algorithm, Sparse Predict and Demote (SPD, a.k.a., “speedy”), and show that it achieves heavy-traffic order-optimality using only a vanishing fraction of one-bit job size queries. It achieves this by lowering the residual demotion barrier—the threshold on remaining service—to create more eligible jobs, then querying jobs at random to keep the demoted fraction at 1−ρ1-\rho. At arrival, the eligible fraction grows relative to this target, allowing the fraction of arriving jobs that are queried to vanish.

In the remainder of this section, we first establish this guarantee when deciding if a job will have a prediction queried for it at arrival, and then consider the case where queries may be delayed until a job has received a chosen amount of service, called the delay trigger. This additional lever can be consequential when predictions are costly (as we establish in Section 5). In both cases, our results characterize how to choose policy parameters (e.g., sampling probabilities and delay triggers) that preserve order-optimality while querying only a vanishing fraction of arrivals. We then use full-size predictions and SRPT scheduling in the low-priority queue to extend the guarantee to the intermediate regime.

Before moving to our main results, we begin by introducing SPD scheduling formally (see Figure 1 for an overview). SPD⁡(b,q,τ,π)\mathrm{SPD}(b,q,\tau,\pi) has four parameters: a residual demotion barrier b≥0b\geq 0 on remaining service, a query probability q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1], a delay trigger τ≥0\tau\geq 0 measured in attained service, and a background scheduling policy π\pi. Under SPD, every job begins at high priority. A job still unfinished at age τ\tau is queried independently with probability qq and is permanently demoted if its remaining service exceeds bb.44 4 Note that each binary query returns only whether the predicted remaining service exceeds the chosen barrier; the full-size variant in Section 4.3 explicitly requests the size itself. The high priority queue uses FCFS and strictly preempts the background queue, which uses π\pi. The defaults are q=1q=1, τ=0\tau=0, and π=FCFS\pi=\mathrm{FCFS}; we omit trailing default arguments, so PD⁡(b)=SPD⁡(b)\mathrm{PD}(b)=\mathrm{SPD}(b). An interesting special case of SPD is the DelayPredict algorithm introduced in [32]. DelayPredict corresponds to SPD⁡(1,1,τ,SRPT)\mathrm{SPD}(1,1,\tau,\mathrm{SRPT}) and was proposed in the context of costly predictions, rather than with the goal of using minimal size information. In Section 4.3 we provide results for the case when SPD uses SRPT scheduling. We compare variations of SPD to DelayPredict outside of heavy traffic in Section 6.

4.1 Sparse Predictions upon Arrival

We first consider sparsity through random sampling at arrival (delay trigger τ=0\tau=0). The goal is to query a vanishing fraction of arrivals while retaining the two properties used in the previous section’s proof of order-optimality: a 1−ρ1-\rho fraction of arrivals is demoted, and each demoted job has size at least a fixed positive fraction of G−1​(ρ)G^{-1}(\rho). The idea is to lower the demotion barrier to make more jobs eligible, then sample arrivals at random. To make the intuition above formal, recall that F¯​(s¯ρ)=1−ρ\overline{F}(\bar{s}_{\rho})=1-\rho and s¯ρ/G−1​(ρ)→θ¯∈(0,1]\bar{s}_{\rho}/G^{-1}(\rho)\to\bar{\theta}\in(0,1] by Lemma 3.4. For a fixed parameter θ∈(0,θ¯)\theta\in(0,\bar{\theta}), we define the θ\theta-tuned residual barrier and the θ\theta-tuned query probability:

bρ​(θ):=θ​G−1​(ρ)a​n​dqρ​(θ):=(1−ρ)/F¯​(bρ​(θ)).b_{\rho}(\theta):=\theta G^{-1}(\rho)\quad and\quad q_{\rho}(\theta):=(1-\rho)/\overline{F}(b_{\rho}(\theta)).\quad

Lowering θ\theta makes more jobs eligible for demotion and reduces the θ\theta-tuned query probability. It also lowers the guaranteed size of a demoted job, but every fixed positive θ\theta retains a lower bound that is a fixed multiple of G−1​(ρ)G^{-1}(\rho), so the demotions still remove enough work from high priority. This probability is valid, with qρ​(θ)∈[0,1]q_{\rho}(\theta)\in[0,1], exactly when bρ​(θ)≤s¯ρb_{\rho}(\theta)\leq\bar{s}_{\rho}. Since θ<θ¯\theta<\bar{\theta}, eventually bρ​(θ)<s¯ρb_{\rho}(\theta)<\bar{s}_{\rho}, and hence qρ​(θ)<1q_{\rho}(\theta)<1.

For the at-arrival policy SPD⁡(bρ​(θ),qρ​(θ))\mathrm{SPD}(b_{\rho}(\theta),q_{\rho}(\theta)) , we draw Qρ​(θ)∼Bernoulli⁡(qρ​(θ))Q_{\rho}(\theta)\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q_{\rho}(\theta)) independently of each job’s size. We query the job if Qρ​(θ)=1Q_{\rho}(\theta)=1 , and assign rank 11 exactly when the queried job has size above bρ​(θ)b_{\rho}(\theta) ; otherwise we assign rank 00. The assigned rank remains fixed, so this policy belongs to the binary-level queue (BLQ) class of Section 3.

Lemma 4.1 (Demotion for θ\theta-tuned parameters).

If qρ​(θ)≤1q_{\rho}(\theta)\leq 1 , the policy SPD⁡(bρ​(θ),qρ​(θ))\mathrm{SPD}(b_{\rho}(\theta),q_{\rho}(\theta)) assigns a 1−ρ1-\rho fraction of arrivals to low priority. Every such job has size greater than bρ​(θ)=θ​G−1​(ρ)b_{\rho}(\theta)=\theta G^{-1}(\rho).

Proof.

Recall that jobs in the low-priority queue have rank 11. The assigned rank is Rρ(θ)=Qρ(θ)𝟏{S>bρ(θ)}R_{\rho}(\theta)=Q_{\rho}(\theta)\mathbf{1}\{S>b_{\rho}(\theta)\}, which gives the size bound. Independence of Qρ​(θ)Q_{\rho}(\theta) and SS also gives ℙ⁡(Rρ​(θ)=1)=qρ​(θ)​F¯​(bρ​(θ))=1−ρ\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}(\theta)=1)=q_{\rho}(\theta)\overline{F}(b_{\rho}(\theta))=1-\rho. ∎

The lemma is the analogue of Lemma 3.3 for the sampled policy. The remaining question is whether the fraction of jobs with remaining size above the barrier grows sufficiently relative to the target 1−ρ1-\rho. The next lemma states that their ratio, which equals 1/qρ​(θ)1/q_{\rho}(\theta) , diverges; taking its reciprocal yields that qρ​(θ)→0q_{\rho}(\theta)\to 0 .

Lemma 4.2 (Abundance below slack-matched threshold).

Suppose the service distribution is in the lognormal-or-lighter regime. For every fixed θ∈(0,θ¯)\theta\in(0,\bar{\theta}), it holds that F¯​(θ​G−1​(ρ))1−ρ⟶∞\frac{\overline{F}(\theta G^{-1}(\rho))}{1-\rho}\longrightarrow\infty.

Proof sketch.

Since θ<θ¯\theta<\bar{\theta}, the residual barrier θ​G−1​(ρ)\theta G^{-1}(\rho) stays a fixed fraction below the slack-matched cutoff s¯ρ\bar{s}_{\rho}. In this regime, the hazard accumulated across that gap grows without bound as the cutoffs increase. Tail probabilities depend exponentially on the cumulative hazard rate, so lowering the cutoff increases the fraction of jobs above the residual barrier by an unbounded factor relative to the target demotion fraction 1−ρ1-\rho. The θ\theta-tuned query probability is the reciprocal of this ratio and, therefore, vanishes. Appendix D.1 gives the full proof. ∎

Equipped with these lemmas, the following theorem shows that predicting every job is unnecessary: the same heavy-traffic order is obtained by querying only a vanishing fraction of arrivals.

Theorem 4.3 (Querying a vanishing fraction of arrivals suffices).

Suppose the service distribution is in the lognormal-or-lighter regime. For every fixed θ∈(0,θ¯)\theta\in(0,\bar{\theta}), the policy SPD⁡(bρ​(θ),qρ​(θ))\mathrm{SPD}(b_{\rho}(\theta),q_{\rho}(\theta)) is well defined for all sufficiently large ρ\rho, has qρ​(θ)→0q_{\rho}(\theta)\to 0 , and is heavy-traffic order-optimal.

Proof.

Lemma 4.2 gives 1/qρ​(θ)→∞1/q_{\rho}(\theta)\to\infty , so theθ\theta-tuned query probabilityqρ​(θ)q_{\rho}(\theta) is eventually valid and tends to zero. By Lemma 4.1, the high-priority slack satisfies

1−λρ𝔼[S𝟏{Rρ(θ)=0}]≥λρ(1−ρ)bρ(θ)=Ω((1−ρ)G−1(ρ)).1-\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}(\theta)=0\}]\geq\lambda_{\rho}(1-\rho)b_{\rho}(\theta)=\Omega\!\left((1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho)\right).

Applying Lemmas 3.1 and 3.2 as in the proof of Theorem 3.5 completes the upper bound. The service moments in these formulas are finite and independent of ρ\rho as discussed in Section 2.1. Lemma 4.1 supplies the required demotion fraction and size scale: both waiting contributions are O⁡(1/((1−ρ)​G−1​(ρ)))O(1/((1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho))), and the residence contributions are O⁡(1)O(1). Finally, SRPT optimality gives 𝔼⁡[TSPD⁡(bρ​(θ),qρ​(θ))]≥𝔼⁡[TSRPT]\mathbb{E}[T^{\mathrm{SPD}(b_{\rho}(\theta),q_{\rho}(\theta))}]\geq\mathbb{E}[T^{\mathrm{SRPT}}]. The SRPT mean response time in (2) supplies the matching lower bound. ∎

4.2 Delayed Prediction Queries

We have established that binary size information for a vanishing fraction of jobs suffices to attain heavy-traffic order-optimality. Until now, this sparsity is achieved by querying jobs at arrival with a θ\theta-tuned query probability qρ​(θ)q_{\rho}(\theta) that vanishes as ρ→1\rho\rightarrow 1. A similar sparsity can also be achieved by delaying the query until only a small fraction of jobs remains unfinished. We thus now consider SPD⁡(b,q,τ)\mathrm{SPD}(b,q,\tau) that also includes a delay trigger τ\tau and requests a prediction with probability qq for any job that reaches age τ\tau, and demotes the job to the low-priority queue if its remaing size exceeds the residual demotion barrier bb.

For each residual barrier bρ​(θ)b_{\rho}(\theta), we seek a range of triggers and associated probabilities that preserve heavy-traffic order-optimality while only querying a vanishing fraction of jobs. To this end, we keep θ∈(0,θ¯)\theta\in(0,\bar{\theta}) fixed and use the residual barrier bρ​(θ)b_{\rho}(\theta) defined above. Then, a fraction F¯​(τ)\overline{F}(\tau) of arrivals remains unfinished at age τ\tau. Among these jobs, the conditional probability of having more than bρ​(θ)b_{\rho}(\theta) units of service left is F¯​(τ+bρ​(θ))/F¯​(τ)\overline{F}(\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta))/\overline{F}(\tau) . Multiplying this with the probability of reaching the trigger gives F¯​(τ+bρ​(θ))\overline{F}(\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta)), fraction of jobs that are large enough for demotion if queried. The sampling rule independently selects a fraction qq of these eligible jobs, so the probability of eventual demotion is q​F¯​(τ+bρ​(θ))q\overline{F}(\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta)). To make the eventually demoted fraction equal to 1−ρ1-\rho, we define the (θ,τ)(\theta,\tau)-tuned query probability

qρ​(θ,τ):=1−ρF¯​(τ+bρ​(θ)).q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau):=\frac{1-\rho}{\overline{F}(\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta))}. (5)

This recovers qρ​(θ,0)=qρ​(θ)q_{\rho}(\theta,0)=q_{\rho}(\theta) at arrival. For 0<θ<θ¯0<\theta<\bar{\theta} and τ≥0\tau\geq 0, we call the pair (θ,τ)(\theta,\tau) feasible at load ρ\rho if qρ​(θ,τ)≤1q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)\leq 1, or equivalently τ+bρ​(θ)≤s¯ρ\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta)\leq\bar{s}_{\rho}. Beyond this point, too few arrivals are eligible to attain the demotion target even with query probability one. For fixed θ∈(0,θ¯)\theta\in(0,\bar{\theta}), the feasible triggers, i.e., those τ\tau for which (θ,τ)(\theta,\tau) is feasible, form the feasible trigger interval [0,τ¯ρ​(θ)][0,\bar{\tau}_{\rho}(\theta)], where τ¯ρ​(θ):=s¯ρ−bρ​(θ)\bar{\tau}_{\rho}(\theta):=\bar{s}_{\rho}-b_{\rho}(\theta). When τ¯ρ​(θ)≥0\bar{\tau}_{\rho}(\theta)\geq 0, its upper endpoint is the latest feasible trigger. This interval is nonempty for all sufficiently large ρ\rho, since Lemma 3.4 and the definition of bρ​(θ)b_{\rho}(\theta) give τ¯ρ​(θ)/G−1​(ρ)=s¯ρ/G−1​(ρ)−θ→θ¯−θ>0\bar{\tau}_{\rho}(\theta)/G^{-1}(\rho)=\bar{s}_{\rho}/G^{-1}(\rho)-\theta\to\bar{\theta}-\theta>0. In this interval we use SPD⁡(bρ​(θ),qρ​(θ,τ),τ)\mathrm{SPD}(b_{\rho}(\theta),q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau),\tau), whose ex-ante query probability 55 5 The query probability qq is conditional on the job remaining unfinished at age τ\tau, that is, on S>τS>\tau. The ex-ante query probability averages over all arrivals, including jobs that finish before the trigger. It therefore captures both the filtering effect of delay and the random selection of jobs that reach the trigger. is

pρqry​(θ,τ):=qρ​(θ,τ)​F¯​(τ)=1−ρF¯​(τ+bρ​(θ))​F¯​(τ).p_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta,\tau):=\text{$q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)\overline{F}(\tau)$}=\frac{1-\rho}{\overline{F}(\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta))}\,\overline{F}(\tau).

This factorization separates the two sources of sparsity. At τ=0\tau=0, sparsity comes entirely from random sampling. At the latest feasible trigger τ=τ¯ρ​(θ)\tau=\bar{\tau}_{\rho}(\theta), the (θ,τ)(\theta,\tau)-tuned query probability is one, so sparsity comes entirely from the small fraction of arrivals that reach the trigger. Intermediate triggers combine the two mechanisms. The next lemma extends Lemma 4.2 from queries at arrival to every trigger in the feasible trigger interval.

Lemma 4.4 (Vanishing ex-ante query probability).

Suppose the service distribution is in the lognormal-or-lighter regime. For each fixed θ∈(0,θ¯)\theta\in(0,\bar{\theta}), the ex-ante query probability vanishes uniformly over the feasible trigger interval:

sup0≤τ≤τ¯ρ​(θ)pρqry​(θ,τ)⟶0as ​ρ→1.\sup_{0\leq\tau\leq\bar{\tau}_{\rho}(\theta)}p_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta,\tau)\longrightarrow 0\quad\text{as }\rho\to 1.
Proof.

A job is queried only if it reaches the trigger and is then selected, so pρqry​(θ,τ)=F¯​(τ)​qρ​(θ,τ)p_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta,\tau)=\overline{F}(\tau)q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau). We split the feasible triggers into two cases. For early triggers, 0≤τ<(θ¯−θ)​G−1​(ρ)/20\leq\tau<(\bar{\theta}-\theta)G^{-1}(\rho)/2, we have τ+bρ​(θ)<(θ¯+θ)​G−1​(ρ)/2\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta)<(\bar{\theta}+\theta)G^{-1}(\rho)/2. Using F¯​(τ)≤1\overline{F}(\tau)\leq 1, we bound the ex-ante query probability by the (θ,τ)(\theta,\tau)-tuned query probability. For late triggers, (θ¯−θ)​G−1​(ρ)/2≤τ≤τ¯ρ​(θ)(\bar{\theta}-\theta)G^{-1}(\rho)/2\leq\tau\leq\bar{\tau}_{\rho}(\theta), feasibility gives qρ​(θ,τ)≤1q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)\leq 1, so we instead bound the ex-ante query probability by the fraction reaching the trigger. Together these bounds give

sup0≤τ≤τ¯ρ​(θ)pρqry​(θ,τ)≤max⁡{1−ρF¯​(θ¯+θ2​G−1​(ρ)),F¯​(θ¯−θ2​G−1​(ρ))}.\sup_{0\leq\tau\leq\bar{\tau}_{\rho}(\theta)}p_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta,\tau)\leq\max\left\{\frac{1-\rho}{\overline{F}\!\left(\frac{\bar{\theta}+\theta}{2}G^{-1}(\rho)\right)},\overline{F}\!\left(\frac{\bar{\theta}-\theta}{2}G^{-1}(\rho)\right)\right\}.

The first bound tends to zero by Lemma 4.2, because (θ¯+θ)/2<θ¯(\bar{\theta}+\theta)/2<\bar{\theta}. The second tends to zero since (θ¯−θ)​G−1​(ρ)/2→∞(\bar{\theta}-\theta)G^{-1}(\rho)/2\to\infty. Both bounds are independent of the particular trigger, giving uniform convergence. ∎

To bound response time, we next quantify the work removed from high priority. As above, we define Qρ​(θ,τ)∼Bernoulli⁡(qρ​(θ,τ))Q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)) as the policy’s size-independent sampling coin, which may equivalently be drawn at arrival and used only if S>τS>\tau. The actual-query indicator is

Qρqry(θ,τ):=Qρ(θ,τ)𝟏{S>τ}.Q_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta,\tau):=Q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)\mathbf{1}\{S>\tau\}.

It equals one exactly when the job reaches the trigger unfinished and is selected for a query, so 𝔼⁡[Qρqry​(θ,τ)]=pρqry​(θ,τ)\mathbb{E}[Q_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta,\tau)]=p_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta,\tau). The eventual demotion indicator is Rρ(θ,τ):=Qρ(θ,τ)𝟏{S>τ+bρ(θ)}.R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau):=Q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)\mathbf{1}\{S>\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta)\}. Here Rρ​(θ,τ)=0R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=0 means the job is never demoted. In particular, if S≤τS\leq\tau, it finishes without a query and has Rρ​(θ,τ)=0R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=0, even when its unused coin has Qρ​(θ,τ)=1Q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=1. A job with Rρ​(θ,τ)=1R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=1 changes from rank zero to rank one upon reaching attained service age τ\tau, while still unfinished. The low-priority service contributed by one arrival is max⁡{0,S−τ}​Rρ​(θ,τ)\max\{0,S-\tau\}R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau). Its first min⁡{S,τ}\min\{S,\tau\} units always receive high priority; the remaining service does so only if the job is never demoted. Accordingly, the high-priority load is

ρρHIGH(θ,τ):=λρ𝔼[min{S,τ}+max{0,S−τ}𝟏{Rρ(θ,τ)=0}].\rho_{\rho}^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\theta,\tau):=\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\min\{S,\tau\}+\max\{0,S-\tau\}\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=0\}\right].
Lemma 4.5 (High-priority slack from demotion).

Suppose the service distribution is in the lognormal-or-lighter regime, and fix θ∈(0,θ¯)\theta\in(0,\bar{\theta}). For every feasible trigger τ\tau, the probability of eventual demotion is ℙ⁡(Rρ​(θ,τ)=1)=1−ρ\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=1)=1-\rho . Uniformly over the feasible trigger interval, 1−ρρHIGH​(θ,τ)=Ω⁡((1−ρ)​G−1​(ρ))1-\rho_{\rho}^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\theta,\tau)=\Omega\!\left((1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho)\right) .

Proof.

A fraction F¯​(τ+bρ​(θ))\overline{F}(\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta)) of arrivals has enough remaining service to qualify for demotion at age τ\tau. The policy samples each such job with probability qρ​(θ,τ)q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau) , independently of size, so

ℙ⁡(Rρ​(θ,τ)=1)=qρ​(θ,τ)​F¯​(τ+bρ​(θ))=1−ρF¯​(τ+bρ​(θ))​F¯​(τ+bρ​(θ))=1−ρ.\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=1)=q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)\overline{F}(\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta))=\frac{1-\rho}{\overline{F}(\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta))}\,\overline{F}(\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta))=1-\rho.

Subtracting the expected low-priority work from the total load therefore yields

1−ρρHIGH​(θ,τ)\displaystyle 1-\rho_{\rho}^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\theta,\tau) =(1−ρ)+λρ​𝔼​[max⁡{0,S−τ}​Rρ​(θ,τ)]≥(1−ρ)+λρ​(1−ρ)​bρ​(θ),\displaystyle=(1-\rho)+\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[\max\{0,S-\tau\}R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)]\geq(1-\rho)+\lambda_{\rho}(1-\rho)b_{\rho}(\theta),

because each eventually demoted job has more than bρ​(θ)b_{\rho}(\theta) service remaining at its demotion time. Since bρ​(θ)=θ​G−1​(ρ)b_{\rho}(\theta)=\theta G^{-1}(\rho) and λρ→1/𝔼⁡[S]>0\lambda_{\rho}\to 1/\mathbb{E}[S]>0 with a fixed finite service mean as noted in Section 2.1, this gives an Ω⁡((1−ρ)​G−1​(ρ))\Omega((1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho)) lower bound, uniformly over the feasible trigger interval. ∎

These lemmas give the bounds needed to extend Theorem 4.3 to delayed predictions.

Theorem 4.6 (Heavy-traffic order-optimality with delayed predictions).

Suppose the service distribution is in the lognormal-or-lighter regime, and fix θ∈(0,θ¯)\theta\in(0,\bar{\theta}). Uniformly over τ\tau in the feasible trigger interval, SPD⁡(bρ​(θ),qρ​(θ,τ),τ)\mathrm{SPD}(b_{\rho}(\theta),q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau),\tau) is heavy-traffic order-optimal and achieves vanishing ex-ante query probability as ρ↑1\rho\uparrow 1.

Proof sketch.

Lemma 4.4 already gives vanishing prediction use. Lemma 4.5 gives the same lower bound on high-priority slack as in the at-arrival proof, while ℙ⁡(Rρ​(θ,τ)=1)=1−ρ\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=1)=1-\rho . If ranks were non-increasing in attained service, Proposition 2.1 and Lemmas 3.1–3.2 would complete the response-time argument just as in Theorem 4.3. For a positive trigger, however, a job that is eventually demoted has its rank increased from zero to one when it reaches the trigger, violating the non-increasing-rank condition of Proposition 2.1.

That said, we can still apply the general SOAP formula in Proposition B.2 separately for jobs that are never demoted and for jobs that are eventually demoted to characterize their corresponding mean response times. The first group includes jobs that finish before the trigger, jobs that finish after the trigger but their residual size then is at most the residual barrier, and jobs that are not sampled for query. The second group includes jobs that are sampled for query at the time of the trigger and have residual size larger than the residual barrier. Weighting the contributions of the groups by ρ\rho and 1−ρ1-\rho, respectively, and using Lemma 4.5 gives the claimed response-time order. Appendix D.2 states the conditional response-time identities for the two groups and combines them with the demotion probability and high-priority slack bound to complete the theorem proof. Appendix D.3 derives those identities from the general SOAP formula. ∎

4.3 Vanishing Full-Size Predictions Suffice for the Intermediate Regime

So far, our upper bounds considered service distributions that are lognormal-or-lighter. In the intermediate regime, Theorem 3.8 rules out heavy-traffic order-optimality for binary-level queues. We now come back to this intermediate regime and show that SPD can obtain heavy-traffic order-optimality in this regime as well if it uses full-size predictions and SRPT scheduling in the low-priority queue.

Theorem 4.7 (Order-optimality with a vanishing fraction of full-size predictions).

Suppose the service distribution is in the intermediate regime or satisfies H⁡(x)∼A​(log⁡x)mH(x)\sim A(\log x)^{m}, with A>0A>0 and m≥2m\geq 2. With full-size predictions, fix any β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1) and set

τρ=F¯−1​((1−ρ)β).\tau_{\rho}=\overline{F}^{-1}\!\left((1-\rho)^{\beta}\right).

Then SPD⁡(τρ,1,τρ,SRPT)\mathrm{SPD}(\tau_{\rho},1,\tau_{\rho},\mathrm{SRPT}) is heavy-traffic order-optimal, with ex-ante query probability (1−ρ)β→0(1-\rho)^{\beta}\to 0.

Although binary-level queues cannot achieve heavy-traffic order-optimality in the intermediate regime, SPD with full-size predictions can do so while querying only a vanishing fraction of arrivals. Specifically, β>0\beta>0 makes the ex-ante query probability vanish, while β<1\beta<1 ensures, under the stated tail assumptions, that enough work is demoted to make the response-time contribution of never-demoted jobs negligible relative to SRPT. Appendix G actually proves a more general result that allows inference costs, which reduces to this theorem when the inference cost is zero.

5 Extension to Costly and Inexact Predictions

Up to this point, our analysis has focused on the setting of free, exact job size predictions. In this section, predictions may require server work and may be inexact. Specifically, each queried job requires δρ≥0\delta_{\rho}\geq 0 units of work on the server to obtain its prediction. This work prevents the server from processing other jobs, so inference causes interference. For a scheduling policy π\pi, let Tπ​(δρ)T^{\pi}(\delta_{\rho}) denote the response time of a typical job, including inference; Tπ​(0)T^{\pi}(0) recovers the free-prediction setting with the same policy parameters.

The inference work described above returns a prediction of the queried job’s total size, which may be inexact. At each load ρ\rho, we describe this output by a prediction rule, a measurable map Φρ:ℝ+×[0,1]→ℝ+\Phi_{\rho}:\mathbb{R}_{+}\times[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}_{+}. For a job of true size SS, its predicted total size is S^=Φρ​(S,U)\widehat{S}=\Phi_{\rho}(S,U), where UU is uniform on [0,1][0,1]. Every job uses the same map with fresh randomness, independent across jobs and of all sizes, arrivals, and sampling coins. A deterministic rule ignores UU. Predictions are ε\varepsilon-inexact if, for a fixed ε∈[0,1)\varepsilon\in[0,1), every job satisfies

(1−ε)​S≤S^≤(1+ε)​S.(1-\varepsilon)S\leq\widehat{S}\leq(1+\varepsilon)S. (6)

Our guarantees are uniform over all prediction rules in this model satisfying the above condition, including biased or randomized rules chosen adversarially at each load. The case ε=0\varepsilon=0 recovers exact predictions. In the remainder of this section, we first study the case of inference costs and exact predictions ε=0\varepsilon=0 in Section 5.1. Section 5.2 then allows for inexact predictions ε>0\varepsilon>0.

5.1 Costly Exact Predictions

When predictions are free, Theorem 4.6 gives heavy-traffic order-optimality for every feasible trigger with a fixed barrier scale θ∈(0,θ¯)\theta\in(0,\bar{\theta}) in the lognormal-or-lighter regime. With costly predictions, SPD keeps a queried job in the high-priority queue until inference finishes, when its prediction determines whether it is demoted. The barrier scale and delay trigger determine how often the server performs this extra work; a high ex-ante query probability can exhaust the available slack or lead to instability. Our main result in this setting shows how to preserve slack and maintain heavy-traffic order-optimality for SPD.

Slack Preservation. To retain the heavy-traffic order-optimality, we need to ensure that a sufficient fraction of the ordinary-service slack remains after adding inference work. To that end, we call a load-dependent pair (θρ,τρ)(\theta_{\rho},\tau_{\rho}) slack-preserving if, for some fixed constant-slack parameter ζ∈(0,1)\zeta\in(0,1), the pair is feasible and satisfies

λρ​δρ​pρqry​(θρ,τρ)≤(1−ζ)​(1−ρ)\lambda_{\rho}\delta_{\rho}p_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta_{\rho},\tau_{\rho})\leq(1-\zeta)(1-\rho) (7)

at all sufficiently high loads. Since the total load is ρ⁡(δρ):=ρ+λρ​δρ​pρqry​(θρ,τρ)\rho(\delta_{\rho}):=\rho+\lambda_{\rho}\delta_{\rho}p_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta_{\rho},\tau_{\rho}), this budget reserves at least ζ⁡(1−ρ)\zeta(1-\rho) slack after inference is included. When predictions are free, ρ⁡(0)=ρ\rho(0)=\rho and every pair that is feasible for all sufficiently high loads is slack-preserving.

Lemma 5.1 (From free to costly predictions).

Fix a constant-slack parameter ζ∈(0,1)\zeta\in(0,1). At a load ρ∈[1/2,1)\rho\in[1/2,1), let π\pi be an SPD policy with FCFS in both queues, a prediction rule, and an ex-ante query probability of at least 1−ρ1-\rho. If π\pi satisfies the slack-preservation condition (7) with this ex-ante query probability, then it is stable and

𝔼⁡[Tπ​(δρ)]≤6ζ2​𝔼​[Tπ​(0)].\mathbb{E}[T^{\pi}(\delta_{\rho})]\leq\frac{6}{\zeta^{2}}\,\mathbb{E}[T^{\pi}(0)].

Lemma 5.1 transfers heavy-traffic order-optimality from free to costly predictions under slack preservation; Appendix E.1 gives its proof. To apply Lemma 5.1 at a given inference cost, we now examine how the trigger choice controls the ex-ante query probability and hence the inference load. At arrival, sparsity comes from random sampling; at the latest feasible trigger, the (θ,τ)(\theta,\tau)-tuned query probability is one, so sparsity comes entirely from the small fraction of jobs that remain unfinished. With costly predictions, the ex-ante query probability induced by the pair (θ,τ)(\theta,\tau) determines the inference load and can separate heavy-traffic order-optimality from instability. To understand which trigger uses fewer queries, consider how often a queried survivor (a job that has size greater than the inference trigger) is eligible for demotion. For a feasible pair (θ,τ)(\theta,\tau), define its self-information by

Iρ​(θ,τ):=−log⁡ℙ⁡(S>τ+bρ​(θ)∣S>τ)=H⁡(τ+bρ​(θ))−H⁡(τ).I_{\rho}(\theta,\tau):=-\log\mathbb{P}(S>\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta)\mid S>\tau)=H(\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta))-H(\tau).

Using the (θ,τ)(\theta,\tau)-tuned query probability in (5), which makes the eventual demotion probability equal to 1−ρ1-\rho, we obtain

pρqry​(θ,τ)=(1−ρ)​eIρ​(θ,τ).p_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta,\tau)=(1-\rho)e^{I_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)}.

Smaller self-information means that a larger fraction of queried jobs can be demoted, so fewer queries are needed to meet the target demotion fraction 1−ρ1-\rho. We use this identity both to choose a trigger and to determine how costly predictions can be while preserving slack.

Self-Information and Trigger Choice.

Fix the service distribution and a parameter θ∈(0,θ¯)\theta\in(0,\bar{\theta}). The following proposition characterizes a trigger that minimizes the ex-ante query probability. We use natural logarithms, so information is measured in nats. When the feasible trigger interval is nonempty, let τρqry​(θ)\tau_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta) denote any trigger in it minimizing pρqry​(θ,τ)p_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta,\tau); the proof below establishes existence.

Proposition 5.2 (Exact trigger objective).

For τ¯ρ​(θ)≥0\bar{\tau}_{\rho}(\theta)\geq 0, a trigger minimizing the ex-ante query probability in the feasible trigger interval [0,τ¯ρ​(θ)][0,\bar{\tau}_{\rho}(\theta)] satisfies

τρqry​(θ)∈arg​min0≤τ≤τ¯ρ​(θ)⁡Iρ​(θ,τ).\tau_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta)\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{0\leq\tau\leq\bar{\tau}_{\rho}(\theta)}I_{\rho}(\theta,\tau).
Proof.

Every trigger in [0,τ¯ρ​(θ)][0,\bar{\tau}_{\rho}(\theta)] paired with the (θ,τ)(\theta,\tau)-tuned query probability gives the same probability of eventual demotion 1−ρ1-\rho. A queried survivor is eligible for demotion exactly when S>τ+bρ​(θ)S>\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta). Since sampling is independent of service size,

ℙ⁡(S>τ+bρ​(θ)∣S>τ)=F¯​(τ+bρ​(θ))F¯​(τ)=e−Iρ​(θ,τ).\mathbb{P}(S>\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta)\mid S>\tau)=\frac{\overline{F}(\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta))}{\overline{F}(\tau)}=e^{-I_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)}.

Thus, the ex-ante query probability equals the target demotion fraction divided by the conditional probability that a queried survivor is eligible for demotion, e−Iρ​(θ,τ)e^{-I_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)}. By the definition of the (θ,τ)(\theta,\tau)-tuned query probability qρ​(θ,τ)q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau),

pρqry​(θ,τ)=qρ​(θ,τ)​F¯​(τ)=(1−ρ)​eIρ​(θ,τ).p_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta,\tau)=q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)\overline{F}(\tau)=(1-\rho)e^{I_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)}.

The exponential map is increasing, so the two minimization problems are equivalent. Since HH is continuous and the feasible trigger interval is nonempty and compact, Iρ​(θ,⋅)I_{\rho}(\theta,\cdot) attains its minimum there. Hence a query-minimizing trigger exists. ∎

With free predictions and fixed θ\theta, every feasible trigger has the same heavy-traffic response-time order. The trigger can therefore be chosen to minimize prediction use. Given that H′=hH^{\prime}=h, ∂Iρ​(θ,τ)∂τ=h⁡(τ+bρ​(θ))−h⁡(τ)\frac{\partial I_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)}{\partial\tau}=h(\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta))-h(\tau), decreasing hazard rates favor delay and increasing hazard rates favor earlier queries.

Inference-Cost Criterion.

Minimizing the ex-ante query probability reduces inference load; yet, for each feasible parameter pair, stability additionally requires λρ​δρ​pρqry​(θρ,τρ)\lambda_{\rho}\delta_{\rho}p_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta_{\rho},\tau_{\rho}) to be less than the ordinary-service slack 1−ρ1-\rho. Preserving a fixed fraction of this slack also permits the response-time comparison in Lemma 5.1. To quantify how inference duration and query choices interact, we use a γ\gamma-exponential cost scale:

λρ​δρ=(1−ρ)γ=e−γ​H​(s¯ρ),γ≥0.\lambda_{\rho}\delta_{\rho}=(1-\rho)^{\gamma}=e^{-\gamma H(\bar{s}_{\rho})},\qquad\gamma\geq 0. (8)

We focus on 0<γ<10<\gamma<1, where queries become cheaper with load but slack shrinks faster.

Each feasible pair (θρ,τρ)(\theta_{\rho},\tau_{\rho}) induces an ex-ante query probability pρqry​(θρ,τρ)p_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta_{\rho},\tau_{\rho}). Multiplying by the arrival rate and the cost per query gives its inference load. Dividing this load by the available slack gives

λρ​δρ​pρqry​(θρ,τρ)1−ρ=exp⁡(Iρ​(θρ,τρ)−γ​H​(s¯ρ)).\frac{\lambda_{\rho}\delta_{\rho}p_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta_{\rho},\tau_{\rho})}{1-\rho}=\exp\!\left(I_{\rho}(\theta_{\rho},\tau_{\rho})-\gamma H(\bar{s}_{\rho})\right). (9)
Lemma 5.3 (γ\gamma-exponential stability criterion).

Suppose the service distribution is in the lognormal-or-lighter regime and we have access to exact predictions at a γ\gamma-exponential cost scale where γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1). For any load-dependent pair (θρ,τρ)(\theta_{\rho},\tau_{\rho}) that is feasible for all sufficiently high loads, we characterize the performance of SPD⁡(bρ​(θρ),qρ​(θρ,τρ),τρ)\mathrm{SPD}(b_{\rho}(\theta_{\rho}),q_{\rho}(\theta_{\rho},\tau_{\rho}),\tau_{\rho}) as follows.

  1. 1.

    Stability. If lim supρ↑1Iρ​(θρ,τρ)H⁡(s¯ρ)<γ\limsup_{\rho\uparrow 1}\frac{I_{\rho}(\theta_{\rho},\tau_{\rho})}{H(\bar{s}_{\rho})}<\gamma then the policy is eventually slack-preserving and stable.

  2. 2.

    Instability. If lim infρ↑1Iρ​(θρ,τρ)H⁡(s¯ρ)>γ\liminf_{\rho\uparrow 1}\frac{I_{\rho}(\theta_{\rho},\tau_{\rho})}{H(\bar{s}_{\rho})}>\gamma then the policy is eventually unstable.

  3. 3.

    Boundary. If Iρ​(θρ,τρ)−γ​H​(s¯ρ)⟶d∈ℝI_{\rho}(\theta_{\rho},\tau_{\rho})-\gamma H(\bar{s}_{\rho})\longrightarrow d\in\mathbb{R} then d<0d<0 gives eventual slack preservation and stability. If d>0d>0, the policy is eventually unstable. For d=0d=0, this limit alone does not determine stability.

Proof of Lemma 5.3.

The inference load is λρ​δρ​pρqry​(θρ,τρ)\lambda_{\rho}\delta_{\rho}p_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta_{\rho},\tau_{\rho}). We compare it with the ordinary-service slack 1−ρ1-\rho using the relative inference load identity (9). Since F¯​(s¯ρ)=1−ρ\overline{F}(\bar{s}_{\rho})=1-\rho by (3), we have H⁡(s¯ρ)=−log⁡(1−ρ)→∞H(\bar{s}_{\rho})=-\log(1-\rho)\to\infty.

Stability. Under the stability condition, some fixed η>0\eta>0 satisfies Iρ​(θρ,τρ)−γ​H​(s¯ρ)≤−η​H​(s¯ρ)I_{\rho}(\theta_{\rho},\tau_{\rho})-\gamma H(\bar{s}_{\rho})\leq-\eta H(\bar{s}_{\rho}) at all sufficiently high loads. The relative inference load therefore satisfies

λρ​δρ​pρqry​(θρ,τρ)1−ρ\displaystyle\frac{\lambda_{\rho}\delta_{\rho}p_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta_{\rho},\tau_{\rho})}{1-\rho} =exp⁡(Iρ​(θρ,τρ)−γ​H​(s¯ρ))≤e−η​H​(s¯ρ)=(1−ρ)η⟶0.\displaystyle=\exp\!\left(I_{\rho}(\theta_{\rho},\tau_{\rho})-\gamma H(\bar{s}_{\rho})\right)\leq e^{-\eta H(\bar{s}_{\rho})}=(1-\rho)^{\eta}\longrightarrow 0.

Hence, the inference load is o⁡(1−ρ)o(1-\rho), giving slack preservation (7) eventually with constant-slack parameter ζ=1/2\zeta=1/2.

Instability. Under the instability condition, the same exponent is at least η​H​(s¯ρ)\eta H(\bar{s}_{\rho}) for some fixed η>0\eta>0 at all sufficiently high loads. The relative inference load is at least (1−ρ)−η→∞(1-\rho)^{-\eta}\to\infty. Inference work eventually exceeds the ordinary-service slack, so total load exceeds one and the policy is unstable.

Boundary. Under the boundary condition, the relative inference load tends to ede^{d}. If d<0d<0, slack preservation (7) holds eventually with constant-slack parameter ζ=(1−ed)/2\zeta=(1-e^{d})/2. If d>0d>0, relative inference load eventually exceeds one, giving instability. If d=0d=0, it tends to one, so no fixed ζ∈(0,1)\zeta\in(0,1) gives slack preservation; finer terms are needed to determine stability. In either slack-preserving case, the total load is eventually at most 1−ζ⁡(1−ρ)<11-\zeta(1-\rho)<1, giving stability. ∎

For a fixed θ∈(0,θ¯)\theta\in(0,\bar{\theta}), Theorem 4.6 gives a common free-prediction response-time order across feasible triggers. Whenever Lemma 5.3 gives slack preservation, Lemma 5.1 transfers this order to the costly policy. We now evaluate the normalized self-information for three tail classes to determine which triggers preserve slack and which cause instability. Here, HH is regularly varying with index ν\nu if H⁡(t​x)/H⁡(x)→tνH(tx)/H(x)\to t^{\nu} as x→∞x\to\infty for every t>0t>0, and rapidly varying if H⁡(t​x)/H⁡(x)→∞H(tx)/H(x)\to\infty as x→∞x\to\infty for every t>1t>1.

Proposition 5.4 (The sparsity mechanism matters).

Fix θ∈(0,θ¯)\theta\in(0,\bar{\theta}) and γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1). Suppose we have access to exact predictions at a γ\gamma-exponential cost scale. Then, depending on the distribution, the selection of the delay trigger can be the difference between heavy-traffic order-optimality and instability of SPD. In particular:

  1. 1.

    If H⁡(x)∼A​(log⁡x)mH(x)\sim A(\log x)^{m}, with A>0A>0 and m≥2m\geq 2, the arrival policy SPD⁡(bρ​(θ),qρ​(θ),0)\mathrm{SPD}(b_{\rho}(\theta),q_{\rho}(\theta),0) is eventually unstable, whereas SPD⁡(bρ​(θ),1,τ¯ρ​(θ))\mathrm{SPD}(b_{\rho}(\theta),1,\bar{\tau}_{\rho}(\theta)), which queries at the latest feasible trigger, is eventually stable and heavy-traffic order-optimal.

  2. 2.

    If HH is rapidly varying, the arrival policy SPD⁡(bρ​(θ),qρ​(θ),0)\mathrm{SPD}(b_{\rho}(\theta),q_{\rho}(\theta),0) is eventually stable and heavy-traffic order-optimal, whereas SPD⁡(bρ​(θ),1,τ¯ρ​(θ))\mathrm{SPD}(b_{\rho}(\theta),1,\bar{\tau}_{\rho}(\theta)) is eventually unstable.

  3. 3.

    If HH is regularly varying with index ν>0\nu>0, fix a∈[0,1−θ)a\in[0,1-\theta) and set τρ=a​G−1​(ρ)\tau_{\rho}=aG^{-1}(\rho). With this trigger, the policy SPD⁡(bρ​(θ),qρ​(θ,τρ),τρ)\mathrm{SPD}(b_{\rho}(\theta),q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau_{\rho}),\tau_{\rho}) is eventually stable and heavy-traffic order-optimal when (a+θ)ν−aν<γ(a+\theta)^{\nu}-a^{\nu}<\gamma, and eventually unstable when (a+θ)ν−aν>γ(a+\theta)^{\nu}-a^{\nu}>\gamma. This threshold decreases with delay for 0<ν<10<\nu<1, increases for ν>1\nu>1, and equals θ\theta for ν=1\nu=1; equality with γ\gamma requires finer asymptotics.

Proof sketch.

Apply Lemma 5.3 to the normalized self-information Iρ​(θ,τρ)/H⁡(s¯ρ)I_{\rho}(\theta,\tau_{\rho})/H(\bar{s}_{\rho}). For polylogarithmic hazards, this ratio tends to 11 at arrival and 00 at the latest trigger. Since 0<γ<10<\gamma<1, the lemma gives instability at arrival and stability at the latest trigger. For rapidly varying hazards, the limits are reversed, so the lemma reverses these conclusions. Under regular variation, the limit at a​G−1​(ρ)aG^{-1}(\rho) is (a+θ)ν−aν(a+\theta)^{\nu}-a^{\nu}; comparing it with γ\gamma in the lemma gives the stated threshold. In each of these stable cases, Lemma 5.3 also gives slack preservation; Theorem 4.6 and Lemma 5.1 then give heavy-traffic order-optimality. Appendices E.4, E.5, and E.6 establish these limits and provide detailed comparisons and full proofs. ∎

5.2 Costly and Inexact Predictions

With free predictions, directly applying the SPD parameters we use for exact-prediction from Section 5.1 to inexact predictions does not yield heavy-traffic order-optimality under systematic underestimation, even for exponential service times (Appendix F.1). In the lognormal-or-lighter regime, lowering the arrival barrier to (1−ε)​bρ​(θ)(1-\varepsilon)b_{\rho}(\theta) with fixed θ∈(0,θ¯)\theta\in(0,\bar{\theta}) restores the guarantee uniformly over the allowed prediction rules (Appendix F.2). This repair leaves the θ\theta-tuned query probability unchanged, so the inference load may still exhaust the ordinary-service slack when predictions are costly. We therefore adjust the barrier at a delayed trigger and choose the delay trigger and θ\theta jointly.

Adjusting the residual barrier at a delayed trigger.

The arrival repair multiplies the true-size cutoff by 1−ε1-\varepsilon. At age τ\tau, that cutoff is τ+bρ​(θ)\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta): we apply the same correction to this total-size threshold, then subtract the τ\tau units already served. This gives the error-adjusted residual demotion barrier

b~ρ​(θ,τ,ε):=(1−ε)​(τ+bρ​(θ))−τ=(1−ε)​bρ​(θ)−ε​τ.\widetilde{b}_{\rho}(\theta,\tau;\varepsilon):=(1-\varepsilon)(\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta))-\tau=(1-\varepsilon)b_{\rho}(\theta)-\varepsilon\tau.

The extra −ε​τ-\varepsilon\tau appears because total size is predicted with error, whereas the completed service τ\tau is known exactly. The test S^−τ>b~ρ​(θ,τ,ε)\widehat{S}-\tau>\widetilde{b}_{\rho}(\theta,\tau;\varepsilon) therefore demotes every queried job with S>τ+bρ​(θ)S>\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta), even under the worst allowed underprediction.

For a feasible pair (θ,τ)(\theta,\tau) with b~ρ​(θ,τ,ε)≥0\widetilde{b}_{\rho}(\theta,\tau;\varepsilon)\geq 0, we run SPD⁡(b~ρ​(θ,τ,ε),qρ​(θ,τ),τ)\mathrm{SPD}(\widetilde{b}_{\rho}(\theta,\tau;\varepsilon),q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau),\tau), keeping the (θ,τ)(\theta,\tau)-tuned query probability as in Section 5.1. Lowering the cutoff can admit smaller jobs, so the candidates below must keep the adjusted residual barrier nonnegative and leave enough ordinary service at demotion. Indeed, a positive prediction satisfies

S−τ>(1−ε)​bρ​(θ)−2​ε​τ1+ε.S-\tau>\frac{(1-\varepsilon)b_{\rho}(\theta)-2\varepsilon\tau}{1+\varepsilon}.

The trigger pair needs to meet two requirements. First, the trigger should be small enough relative to the barrier so that even when the barrier is lowered, we can ensure every demoted job retains at least a fixed fraction of G−1​(ρ)G^{-1}(\rho) units of service. Second, the pair must induce sufficiently few queries so that inference is slack-preserving. Our construction achieves this balance by identifying a family of candidate pairs that all satisfy the first requirement (Lemma 5.5) and at least one satisfies the second requirement (Lemma 5.6).

A finite list of candidate pairs.

Fix an integer N≥2N\geq 2. For 1≤j≤N1\leq j\leq N, set

τρ,j:=θ¯2​(1−ε2​(1+ε))j​G−1​(ρ)a​n​dθj:=(1+3​ε)​θ¯2​(1−ε)​(1−ε2​(1+ε))j.\tau_{\rho,j}:=\frac{\bar{\theta}}{2}\left(\frac{1-\varepsilon}{2(1+\varepsilon)}\right)^{j}G^{-1}(\rho)\qquad and\qquad\theta_{j}:=\frac{(1+3\varepsilon)\bar{\theta}}{2(1-\varepsilon)}\left(\frac{1-\varepsilon}{2(1+\varepsilon)}\right)^{j}.

Candidate jj uses trigger τρ,j\tau_{\rho,j} and a correspondingly tuned query probability qρ​(θj,τρ,j)q_{\rho}(\theta_{j},\tau_{\rho,j}), and error-adjusted residual demotion barrier b~ρ​(θj,τρ,j,ε)\widetilde{b}_{\rho}(\theta_{j},\tau_{\rho,j};\varepsilon). In particular,

bρ​(θj)=1+3​ε1−ε​τρ,jandb~ρ​(θj,τρ,j,ε)=(1+2​ε)​τρ,j.b_{\rho}(\theta_{j})=\frac{1+3\varepsilon}{1-\varepsilon}\tau_{\rho,j}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\widetilde{b}_{\rho}(\theta_{j},\tau_{\rho,j};\varepsilon)=(1+2\varepsilon)\tau_{\rho,j}. (10)

The first identity in (10) follows by cancelling the common geometric factor in θj\theta_{j} and τρ,j\tau_{\rho,j}; substitution into (1−ε)​bρ​(θj)−ε​τρ,j(1-\varepsilon)b_{\rho}(\theta_{j})-\varepsilon\tau_{\rho,j} gives the second. A demoted job therefore satisfies

(1+ε)​S≥S^>τρ,j+b~ρ​(θj,τρ,j,ε)=2​(1+ε)​τρ,j.(1+\varepsilon)S\geq\widehat{S}>\tau_{\rho,j}+\widetilde{b}_{\rho}(\theta_{j},\tau_{\rho,j};\varepsilon)=2(1+\varepsilon)\tau_{\rho,j}.

As a result, it retains S−τρ,j>τρ,jS-\tau_{\rho,j}>\tau_{\rho,j} ordinary service, as required by the next lemma.

Lemma 5.5 (Every candidate works with free predictions).

Suppose the service distribution is in the lognormal-or-lighter regime, and fix ε∈[0,1)\varepsilon\in[0,1) and N≥2N\geq 2. All candidate pairs are feasible for all sufficiently high loads. Under free ε\varepsilon-inexact predictions, their corresponding policies have vanishing ex-ante query probabilities and are heavy-traffic order-optimal.

Proof sketch.

The candidate endpoints τρ,j+bρ​(θj)\tau_{\rho,j}+b_{\rho}(\theta_{j}) are eventually below s¯ρ\bar{s}_{\rho}, giving feasibility of the candidate pairs. Their adjusted barriers are nonnegative by (10), so the policies are well defined at these loads; their diverging triggers give vanishing ex-ante query probabilities. For candidate jj, write τ=τρ,j\tau=\tau_{\rho,j} and let pp be the demoted fraction and ρHIGH​(0)\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(0) be this candidate’s high-priority load with free predictions. The adjusted test gives p≥1−ρp\geq 1-\rho and leaves every demoted job more than τ\tau service.

For high priority, demotion removes at least p​τp\tau service per arrival, giving slack at least λρ​p​τ≥λρ​(1−ρ)​τ\lambda_{\rho}p\tau\geq\lambda_{\rho}(1-\rho)\tau. Jobs that stay in high priority thus contribute at most order 1/((1−ρ)​τ)1/((1-\rho)\tau) to mean response time. For jobs sent to low priority (as shown in Appendix F.4), the leading response-time term is at most a constant times

p(1−ρ)​(1−ρHIGH​(0))≤p(1−ρ)​λρ​p​τ=1λρ​(1−ρ)​τ.\frac{p}{(1-\rho)\,(1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(0))}\leq\frac{p}{(1-\rho)\lambda_{\rho}p\tau}=\frac{1}{\lambda_{\rho}(1-\rho)\tau}.

The remaining service term stays bounded: averaged over arrivals, residual work also adds proportionally to high-priority slack, and each demoted job’s service before demotion is smaller than its residual work. Finally, τ=Θ​(G−1​(ρ))\tau=\Theta(G^{-1}(\rho)), so both groups’ contributions have the SRPT upper-bound scale. Appendix F.3 gives the full calculation, matching lower bound, and uniformity argument. ∎

Lemma 5.6 (At least one candidate preserves slack).

For the service distribution and error bound of Lemma 5.5, fix γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1) and an integer N>1/γN>1/\gamma, and use the candidate pairs above with the γ\gamma-exponential cost scale (8). At every sufficiently high load, some candidate preserves slack, uniformly over the allowed prediction rules.

Proof.

Note that τρ,j+1+bρ​(θj+1)=τρ,j+1+1+3​ε1−ε​τρ,j+1=2​(1+ε)1−ε​τρ,j+1=τρ,j\tau_{\rho,j+1}+b_{\rho}(\theta_{j+1})=\tau_{\rho,j+1}+\frac{1+3\varepsilon}{1-\varepsilon}\tau_{\rho,j+1}=\frac{2(1+\varepsilon)}{1-\varepsilon}\tau_{\rho,j+1}=\tau_{\rho,j}. As a result, the intervals [τρ,j,τρ,j+bρ​(θj)][\tau_{\rho,j},\tau_{\rho,j}+b_{\rho}(\theta_{j})] are adjacent, for 1≤j<N1\leq j<N and their hazard increments thus telescope:

∑j=1NIρ​(θj,τρ,j)=H⁡(θ¯2​G−1​(ρ))−H⁡(τρ,N)≤H⁡(s¯ρ)=−log⁡(1−ρ).\sum_{j=1}^{N}I_{\rho}(\theta_{j},\tau_{\rho,j})=H\!\left(\frac{\bar{\theta}}{2}G^{-1}(\rho)\right)-H(\tau_{\rho,N})\leq H(\bar{s}_{\rho})=-\log(1-\rho).

The last inequality uses H⁡(⋅)≥0H(\cdot)\geq 0 and the largest candidate endpoint being at most s¯ρ\bar{s}_{\rho} at sufficiently high loads. Hence, there exists a candidate jj such that Iρ​(θj,τρ,j)≤−log⁡(1−ρ)NI_{\rho}(\theta_{j},\tau_{\rho,j})\leq\frac{-\log(1-\rho)}{N}. This implies that pρqry​(θj,τρ,j)=(1−ρ)​eIρ​(θj,τρ,j)≤(1−ρ)1−1/N.p_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta_{j},\tau_{\rho,j})=(1-\rho)e^{I_{\rho}(\theta_{j},\tau_{\rho,j})}\leq(1-\rho)^{1-1/N}. Given that N>1/γN>1/\gamma, candidate jj satisfies slack preservation (7) as its inference load relative to the available slack eventually vanishes: λρ​δρ​pρqry​(θj,τρ,j)1−ρ≤(1−ρ)γ−1/N⟶0.\frac{\lambda_{\rho}\delta_{\rho}p_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta_{j},\tau_{\rho,j})}{1-\rho}\leq(1-\rho)^{\gamma-1/N}\longrightarrow 0. The above construction does not rely on a particular prediction rule, so this candidate preserves slack uniformly over all allowed prediction rules. ∎

Self-Information and Affordability.

Finding one true-size candidate among queried survivors takes eIρ​(θ,τ)e^{I_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)} queries on average. Spending all available slack on inference would permit eγ​H​(s¯ρ)e^{\gamma H(\bar{s}_{\rho})} queries per such candidate. The choice N>1/γN>1/\gamma makes the selected candidate’s query demand a vanishing fraction of this allowance. Combining this slack preservation with Lemmas 5.1 and 5.5 gives the following theorem.

Theorem 5.7 (Robustness with costly inference).

Suppose the service distribution is in the lognormal-or-lighter regime. For every ε∈[0,1)\varepsilon\in[0,1) and γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1), under the γ\gamma-exponential cost scale (8), there is a load-dependent pair (θρ,τρ)(\theta_{\rho},\tau_{\rho}), feasible for all sufficiently high loads, for which SPD⁡(b~ρ​(θρ,τρ,ε),qρ​(θρ,τρ),τρ)\mathrm{SPD}\bigl(\widetilde{b}_{\rho}(\theta_{\rho},\tau_{\rho};\varepsilon),q_{\rho}(\theta_{\rho},\tau_{\rho}),\tau_{\rho}\bigr) is eventually stable, has vanishing ex-ante query probability, and is heavy-traffic order-optimal, uniformly over all ε\varepsilon-inexact rules.

Proof.

Fix N=⌊1/γ⌋+1N=\lfloor 1/\gamma\rfloor+1. At each sufficiently high load, we choose the smallest qualifying index jρj_{\rho} in Lemma 5.6 and set (θρ,τρ)=(θjρ,τρ,jρ)(\theta_{\rho},\tau_{\rho})=(\theta_{j_{\rho}},\tau_{\rho,j_{\rho}}). Lemma 5.5 gives a uniform free-prediction bound for all candidates, and Lemma 5.6 makes the selected pair slack-preserving. Lemma 5.1 establishes eventual stability and transfers the heavy-traffic order to the costly policy. The selected ex-ante query probability also vanishes by the query bound in the proof of Lemma 5.6. ∎

Finding the pair.

For fixed ε\varepsilon and γ\gamma, the candidate tuning constants are computed once. At each sufficiently high load, evaluate the hazard increments for at most ⌊1/γ⌋+1\lfloor 1/\gamma\rfloor+1 candidates and select the first qualifying one. Hence, selection uses O⁡(1/γ)O(1/\gamma) distribution evaluations and is independent of the realized prediction errors.

6 Numerical Experiments

Our analytic results focus on the heavy-traffic regime; however, the resulting insights into policy design also apply at moderate loads. In this section, we show that the design choices that provide heavy-traffic order-optimality for SPD also yield near-optimal performance outside heavy traffic.

Experimental Setup.

Our numerical experiments use the closed-form expressions for SPD derived in this work. We consider Poisson arrivals and mean-one service times from the following distributions: doubly exponential, exponential, Weibull with ν=0.5,2\nu=0.5,2, and lognormal with σ=1\sigma=1. Unless otherwise stated, predictions are costly and exact; each query consumes server time δρ\delta_{\rho}, chosen so that λρ​δρ=1−ρ\lambda_{\rho}\delta_{\rho}=\sqrt{1-\rho}. At each load, we independently tune (τ,b,q)(\tau,b,q) over the full family of stable SPD policies for each background scheduler. As baselines, we compare against two size-oblivious policies: FCFS and FB, which are optimal for distributions with increasing and decreasing hazard rates, respectively. We also compare with DelayPredict [32], implemented as SPD⁡(0,1,τ,SRPT)\mathrm{SPD}(0,1,\tau,\mathrm{SRPT}) which demotes all queried jobs and runs SRPT on the low-priority queue.

Performance Inside and Outside Heavy Traffic.

Figure 2 compares SPD with FCFS, FB, and DelayPredict, with response times normalized by SRPT with free size information. Over moderate loads 0.85≤ρ≤0.990.85\leq\rho\leq 0.99, SPD stays within a small multiple of this optimum across all four distributions: the largest observed ratios are 4.72 for SPD(FCFS) and 4.00 for SPD(SRPT). All policies perform comparably for exponential service, but the size-oblivious policies are more sensitive to the service distribution: FB performs poorly for doubly exponential service, whereas FCFS performs poorly for Weibull ν=0.5\nu=0.5 and lognormal service. SPD avoids these pronounced losses across the four examples, although FB can outperform it at some moderate loads.

At high loads, SPD continues to perform well across all four distributions. Over the grid through ρ=1−10−8\rho=1-10^{-8}, its largest observed response ratios are 5.71 for SPD(FCFS) and 4.11 for SPD(SRPT). By comparison, FB’s ratio reaches 51.86 for doubly exponential service, while FCFS’s reaches 286.17 and 424.75 for Weibull ν=0.5\nu=0.5 and lognormal service. At the highest plotted load, both SPD variants outperform both size-oblivious baselines in all four examples, while each queries at most 1.42×10−51.42\times 10^{-5} of arrivals.

DelayPredict is competitive at moderate loads and nearly matches SPD(SRPT) at high loads for Weibull ν=0.5\nu=0.5 and lognormal service. In these cases, tuning SPD(SRPT) selects q=1q=1 and a trigger close to DelayPredict’s, so both obtain sparsity by delaying queries. However, for doubly exponential service, both SPD variants improve substantially on DelayPredict: at ρ=1−10−8\rho=1-10^{-8}, the response ratios are 5.10 for DelayPredict, 1.89 for SPD(FCFS), and 1.53 for SPD(SRPT). Here SPD benefits from querying a small fraction of jobs at arrival, while DelayPredict can limit query use only by delaying the trigger.

Trigger Selection.

Figure 3 illustrates how the best trigger depends on the service distribution outside of heavy traffic. In this figure, we set ρ=0.9\rho=0.9 and b=0.1​G−1​(ρ)b=0.1G^{-1}(\rho), and adjust qq as the trigger varies to keep q​F¯​(τ+b)=1−ρq\overline{F}(\tau+b)=1-\rho, fixing the fraction of arrivals demoted. We normalize the trigger by τmax=τ¯ρ​(0.1)=F−1​(ρ)−b\tau_{\max}=\bar{\tau}_{\rho}(0.1)=F^{-1}(\rho)-b. The best trigger is at arrival for Weibull ν=2\nu=2 and is the latest feasible trigger for ν=0.5\nu=0.5, both with free and with costly predictions.

These curves reflect two effects of trigger choice. Although each demoted job has more than bb units of service remaining, the mean 𝔼⁡[S−τ∣S>τ+b]\mathbb{E}[S-\tau\mid S>\tau+b] depends on τ\tau. For Weibull ν=0.5\nu=0.5, an earlier trigger demotes less remaining work per job and requires more queries to demote the same 1−ρ1-\rho fraction; for ν=2\nu=2, a later trigger has both disadvantages. The first effect changes priority allocation even with free predictions; the second adds inference load when predictions are costly. For Weibull ν=0.5\nu=0.5, inference cost makes the first 17.35% of the trigger range unstable. Thus an incorrect trigger can more than double delay or destroy stability even at the moderate load ρ=0.9\rho=0.9. The figure uses FCFS as the background scheduler; SRPT gives qualitatively similar results.

7 Concluding Remarks

A fundamental challenge for scheduling is to determine the minimal information about job sizes necessary to achieve near-optimal mean response times in a single-server queue. We introduced a novel policy called Sparse Predict and Demote (SPD), which can achieve heavy-traffic order-optimality, even in situations with costly and/or inexact predictions, using a vanishing fraction of one-bit job-size predictions. Although our analytic guarantees concern the heavy-traffic regime, we use numerical experiments to show that the insights extend beyond heavy traffic. Importantly, our results highlight both when a vanishing fraction of one-bit predictions is enough to achieve heavy-traffic order-optimality and when one-bit predictions are not enough. Our work also points to several avenues of open direction described below.

First, the intermediate regime leaves an unresolved gap in the amount of size information needed to achieve heavy-traffic order-optimality. Our impossibility result applies to binary-level queues, while the positive result requires full-size information to order demoted jobs by remaining size. An open question is whether a fixed number of size classes can replace these full-size predictions while retaining both heavy-traffic order-optimality and a vanishing query fraction. Resolving this gap would clarify the prediction precision required by different service distributions.

Second, it would be desirable to relax the current M/GI/1 assumption; that is, extend sparse prediction to queues with more than one server or non-Poisson arrivals. For renewal arrivals, the diffusion analysis of two-priority-class queues by Chen and Dong [7] provides a possible starting point. The challenge is to obtain comparable guarantees for mean response time in these models while accounting for inference work and querying only a vanishing fraction of jobs.

Finally, our robustness analysis gives sufficient conditions for heavy-traffic order-optimality under a fixed multiplicative error bound, leaving open how much error can be tolerated. It also does not exploit improvements in prediction quality over time. As more accurate predictions become available, the policy could adjust when it queries jobs and how it uses the resulting estimates. It remains open when such adaptations reduce inference work or mean response time while preserving heavy-traffic order-optimality.

Appendix A Consequences of Assumption 1 (Section 2.1)

We organize the consequences of Assumption 1 into three parts: finite service-time moments in Appendix A.1, the boundary of the lognormal-or-lighter regime in Appendix A.2, and tail-work estimates in Appendix A.3.

A.1 Finite Service-Time Moments

The response-time formulas throughout the paper depend on the first two service-time moments. The following lemma ensures that these moments are finite constants as the load approaches one; in particular, it justifies the FCFS benchmark in Appendix B.1.

Lemma A.1 (Finite service-time moments).

Under Assumption 1, 0<𝔼⁡[Sm]<∞0<\mathbb{E}[S^{m}]<\infty for every m>0m>0. These moments are independent of ρ\rho, since the service distribution is fixed in the heavy-traffic limit.

Proof of Lemma A.1.

Fix m>0m>0. Since H⁡(x)/log⁡x→∞H(x)/\log x\to\infty (by the first condition of Assumption 1), there exists an x0>1x_{0}>1 such that H⁡(x)≥(m+1)​log⁡xH(x)\geq(m+1)\log x, and hence F¯​(x)≤x−(m+1)\overline{F}(x)\leq x^{-(m+1)}, for every x≥x0x\geq x_{0}. The tail-integral identity gives

𝔼⁡[Sm]=m​∫0∞xm−1​F¯​(x)​𝑑x≤x0m+m​∫x0∞x−2​𝑑x<∞.\mathbb{E}[S^{m}]=m\int_{0}^{\infty}x^{m-1}\overline{F}(x)\,dx\leq x_{0}^{m}+m\int_{x_{0}}^{\infty}x^{-2}\,dx<\infty.

The moments are positive because the service distribution has unbounded support. Their constancy in ρ\rho follows from holding this distribution fixed. ∎

A.2 Lognormal-or-Lighter Boundary

The classification below supplies the hazard lower bound used in Appendix D.1 (Section 4), so we collect these distributional consequences here. We define

L:=limx→∞x​h​(x)log⁡x∈[0,∞],L:=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{xh(x)}{\log x}\in[0,\infty],

which exists by the third condition of Assumption 1. We now use LL to classify the regimes in Section 2.1.

Lemma A.2 (Lognormal boundary).

Under Assumption 1, LL determines the tail regime:

  1. 1.

    If L=0L=0, then log⁡x≪H⁡(x)≪(log⁡x)2\log x\ll H(x)\ll(\log x)^{2} , i.e., the service distribution is in the intermediate regime.

  2. 2.

    If 0<L<∞0<L<\infty, then H⁡(x)∼L2​(log⁡x)2H(x)\sim\frac{L}{2}(\log x)^{2}, i.e., the lognormal boundary.

  3. 3.

    If L=∞L=\infty, then H⁡(x)/(log⁡x)2→∞H(x)/(\log x)^{2}\to\infty, i.e., the service distribution is lognormal-or-lighter.

Proof of Lemma A.2.

By the first condition of Assumption 1, H⁡(x)log⁡x⟶∞\frac{H(x)}{\log x}\longrightarrow\infty, so in particular H⁡(x)→∞H(x)\to\infty. Since H′​(x)=h​(x)H^{\prime}(x)=h(x), the rule of de l’Hôpital gives

limx→∞H⁡(x)(log⁡x)2=limx→∞h⁡(x)2​log⁡x/x=12​limx→∞x​h​(x)log⁡x=L2.\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{H(x)}{(\log x)^{2}}=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{h(x)}{2\log x/x}=\frac{1}{2}\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{xh(x)}{\log x}=\frac{L}{2}.

This proves the limit in all three cases L=0L=0, 0<L<∞0<L<\infty, and L=∞L=\infty, and hence the stated classification. ∎

A.3 Tail-Work Estimates

The following estimates convert the probability of exceeding a cutoff into the expected work carried by those jobs. The constant-factor bound is used for the tail-work scarcity estimate in Appendix C.5; the sharper asymptotic is used to compare the size and workload cutoffs in Appendix C.3. For a cutoff x>0x>0, the baseline x​F¯​(x)x\overline{F}(x) counts xx units of service for each job exceeding the cutoff. The remaining service is the tail integral:

𝔼[S𝟏{S>x}]=xF¯(x)+∫x∞F¯(u)du.\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{S>x\}]=x\overline{F}(x)+\int_{x}^{\infty}\overline{F}(u)\,du.

The first estimate bounds the excess by a constant multiple of the baseline; the second shows that it is negligible in the lognormal-or-lighter regime.

Lemma A.3 (Tail-work bound).

Under Assumption 1, as x→∞x\to\infty,

𝔼[S𝟏{S>x}]=Θ(xF¯(x)).\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{S>x\}]=\Theta\!\left(x\overline{F}(x)\right).
Proof of Lemma A.3.

The second condition of Assumption 1, α⁡(F¯)<−2\alpha(\overline{F})<-2 provides a bound that is uniform over every larger threshold. Choose p>2p>2 with α⁡(F¯)<−p\alpha(\overline{F})<-p. By the definition in the footnote to the second condition of Assumption 1, there exist C<∞C<\infty and x0<∞x_{0}<\infty such that

F¯​(x​y)F¯​(x)≤C​y−p,x≥x0,y≥1.\frac{\overline{F}(xy)}{\overline{F}(x)}\leq Cy^{-p},\qquad x\geq x_{0},\quad y\geq 1.

Changing variables from uu to x​yxy therefore gives

∫x∞F¯​(u)​𝑑u=x​∫1∞F¯​(x​y)​𝑑y≤Cp−1​x​F¯​(x).\int_{x}^{\infty}\overline{F}(u)\,du=x\int_{1}^{\infty}\overline{F}(xy)\,dy\leq\frac{C}{p-1}x\overline{F}(x).

Thus the excess work can enlarge the baseline x​F¯​(x)x\overline{F}(x) by at most a fixed factor:

xF¯(x)≤𝔼[S𝟏{S>x}]≤(1+Cp−1)xF¯(x).x\overline{F}(x)\leq\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{S>x\}]\leq\left(1+\frac{C}{p-1}\right)x\overline{F}(x).

This proves the claimed Θ\Theta estimate. ∎

In the lognormal-or-lighter regime, the mean excess size above a high cutoff is 𝔼⁡[S−x∣S>x]=o⁡(x)\mathbb{E}[S-x\mid S>x]=o(x). Thus a job exceeding xx has mean size asymptotic to xx, and the total work in such jobs is asymptotic to xx times their probability. The explicit factor 22 below is sufficient for the cutoff comparison in Appendix C.3.

Lemma A.4 (Tail-work asymptotics).

In the lognormal-or-lighter regime, as x→∞x\to\infty,

𝔼[S𝟏{S>x}]=xF¯(x)(1+o(1)).\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{S>x\}]=x\overline{F}(x)(1+o(1)).

In particular, for all sufficiently large xx,

xF¯(x)≤𝔼[S𝟏{S>x}]≤2xF¯(x).x\overline{F}(x)\leq\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{S>x\}]\leq 2x\overline{F}(x).
Proof of Lemma A.4.

In the lognormal-or-lighter regime, the bound on relative tail probabilities becomes stronger as the threshold grows. By Lemma A.2, L∈(0,∞]L\in(0,\infty], so there is a c>0c>0 such that h⁡(u)≥c​log⁡u/uh(u)\geq c\log u/u for all sufficiently large uu. For large xx and every y≥1y\geq 1, this gives

H⁡(x​y)−H⁡(x)≥c​∫xx​ylog⁡uu​𝑑u≥c​log​x​log​y,F¯​(x​y)F¯​(x)≤y−c​log⁡x.H(xy)-H(x)\geq c\int_{x}^{xy}\frac{\log u}{u}\,du\geq c\log x\log y,\qquad\frac{\overline{F}(xy)}{\overline{F}(x)}\leq y^{-c\log x}.

Unlike the fixed exponent pp in the previous proof, the exponent c​log⁡xc\log x tends to infinity.

We again start with the integral of F¯\overline{F} from xx to infinity and change variables from uu to x​yxy. Once c​log⁡x>1c\log x>1, the tail bound above gives

∫x∞F¯​(u)​du=x​∫1∞F¯​(x​y)​dy≤x​F¯​(x)​∫1∞y−c​log⁡x​dy=x​F¯​(x)c​log⁡x−1=o⁡(x​F¯​(x)).\displaystyle\int_{x}^{\infty}\overline{F}(u)\,du=x\int_{1}^{\infty}\overline{F}(xy)\,dy\leq x\overline{F}(x)\int_{1}^{\infty}y^{-c\log x}\,dy=\frac{x\overline{F}(x)}{c\log x-1}=o\!\left(x\overline{F}(x)\right).

The last step follows because 1/(c​log⁡x−1)→01/(c\log x-1)\to 0. Thus the expected service beyond the threshold is negligible compared with the baseline work x​F¯​(x)x\overline{F}(x). Substituting this estimate into the tail-work decomposition yields

𝔼[S𝟏{S>x}]=xF¯(x)+∫x∞F¯(u)du=xF¯(x)+o(xF¯(x))=xF¯(x)(1+o(1)).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{S>x\}]=x\overline{F}(x)+\int_{x}^{\infty}\overline{F}(u)\,du=x\overline{F}(x)+o\!\left(x\overline{F}(x)\right)=x\overline{F}(x)(1+o(1)).

This proves the asymptotic statement. For all sufficiently large xx, the excess integral is at most x​F¯​(x)x\overline{F}(x), giving the upper bound with factor 22; the lower bound follows from the nonnegative excess integral.

∎

Appendix B FCFS Benchmark and SOAP Response-Time (Section 2.2)

Appendix B.1 derives the FCFS mean response time from the SOAP identity and compares its heavy-traffic order with SRPT. Appendix B.2 then states the general SOAP response-time identity and explains how it accounts for changes in priority as jobs receive service.

B.1 FCFS Benchmark

With no inference work, FCFS has the constant rank r⁡(d,a)=0r(d,a)=0. An older job contributes all its service to the original relevant interval, while a new arrival cannot pass the tagged job in an FCFS tie. Consequently,

X0old​[0]=S,Xiold​[0]=0​(i≥1),Xnew​[0]=0.X_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[0]=S,\qquad X_{i}^{\mathrm{old}}[0]=0\ (i\geq 1),\qquad X^{\mathrm{new}}[0]=0.

The corresponding loads are ρ0old​[0]=ρ\rho_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[0]=\rho and ρnew​[0]=0\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[0]=0. Substitution in Proposition 2.1 gives, for a tagged job of size xx,

𝔼⁡[Td,x]=λρ​𝔼​[S2]2​(1−ρ)+x.\mathbb{E}[T_{d,x}]=\frac{\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[S^{2}]}{2(1-\rho)}+x.

Averaging over x=Sx=S gives

𝔼⁡[TFCFS]=𝔼⁡[S]+λρ​𝔼​[S2]2​(1−ρ).\mathbb{E}[T^{\mathrm{FCFS}}]=\mathbb{E}[S]+\frac{\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[S^{2}]}{2(1-\rho)}.

By Lemma A.1, the service moments are fixed positive constants and λρ→1/𝔼⁡[S]>0\lambda_{\rho}\to 1/\mathbb{E}[S]>0, so its mean response time has order (1−ρ)−1(1-\rho)^{-1}. Comparing with (2) gives 𝔼⁡[TFCFS]/𝔼⁡[TSRPT]=Θ⁡(G−1​(ρ))\mathbb{E}[T^{\mathrm{FCFS}}]/\mathbb{E}[T^{\mathrm{SRPT}}]=\Theta(G^{-1}(\rho)).

B.2 General SOAP Identity and Intuition

Proposition 2.1 assumes that a job’s rank does not increase as it receives service. This assumption need not hold when a policy requests a size prediction only after a job has received some service: the prediction may cause the job to be assigned lower priority, increasing its rank. We therefore also need a characterization of the mean response time for general rank trajectories. For a generic arriving job with descriptor DD and total server work XX, let Xnew​[r]X^{\mathrm{new}}[r] denote the service received until the job completes or first has rank at least rr; this variable is zero if the job arrives with rank at least rr. As in Section 2.2, define ρnew​[r]:=λ​𝔼​[Xnew​[r]]\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[r]:=\lambda\mathbb{E}[X^{\mathrm{new}}[r]]. The pairs (D,X)(D,X) are i.i.d. across jobs and independent of the Poisson arrival process.

For general ranks, we need two additions to the notation. First, an old job may enter the region relevant to rank rr multiple times. We let X0old​[r]X_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[r] denote its service in the original relevant interval and Xiold​[r]X_{i}^{\mathrm{old}}[r], i≥1i\geq 1, its service in the ii-th recycled relevant interval, and define ρiold​[r]:=λ​𝔼​[Xiold​[r]], where ​i≥0\rho_{i}^{\mathrm{old}}[r]:=\lambda\mathbb{E}[X_{i}^{\mathrm{old}}[r]],\text{ where }i\geq 0. Second, the tagged job’s current rank need not capture all work that can delay it, because its rank may worsen later. SOAP therefore uses its worst future rank rd,xworst​(a):=supa≤b<xr⁡(d,b)r_{d,x}^{\mathrm{worst}}(a):=\sup_{a\leq b<x}r(d,b).

With these definitions, the general SOAP response-time identity is as follows.

Proposition B.2 (SOAP for general ranks [28, Theorem 5.5]).

The conditional mean response time of a tagged job with descriptor dd and total work xx is

𝔼⁡[Td,x]=λ​∑i=0∞𝔼⁡[(Xiold​[r])2]2​(1−ρ0old​[r])​(1−ρnew​[r])+∫0xd​a1−ρnew​[r​(a)],\mathbb{E}[T_{d,x}]=\frac{\lambda\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\mathbb{E}\!\left[(X_{i}^{\mathrm{old}}[r])^{2}\right]}{2(1-\rho_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[r])(1-\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[r])}+\int_{0}^{x}\frac{da}{1-\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[r(a)]},

where r=rd,xworst​(0)r=r_{d,x}^{\mathrm{worst}}(0) and r⁡(a)=rd,xworst​(a)r(a)=r_{d,x}^{\mathrm{worst}}(a).

We provide some additional intuition for Proposition B.2, focusing on the two features that arise when ranks are not monotone in age.

The first issue is that the tagged job’s current rank need not determine all of the work that can delay it. Even if another job has lower priority than the tagged job at its current rank, it may still delay the tagged job if the tagged job’s own rank becomes worse later. The Pessimism Principle of [28] shows that, when determining how much another job can delay a tagged job of descriptor dd and total work xx at age aa, it suffices to compare that job against the tagged job’s worst future rank, defined above. More strongly, the Worst Future Rank Substitution result of [28, Appendix D] shows that the tagged job may be scheduled as if its rank at every age aa were rd,xworst​(a)r_{d,x}^{\mathrm{worst}}(a), while leaving the arrival sequence and the rank functions of all other jobs unchanged, without changing the tagged job’s response time. Since a↦rd,xworst​(a)a\mapsto r_{d,x}^{\mathrm{worst}}(a) is non-increasing, this gives an equivalent non-increasing-rank representation from the perspective of the tagged job. Intuitively, the substitution pessimistically gives the tagged job immediately the worst priority that it will attain in the future; doing so does not change which pieces of competing work ultimately delay its completion.

The second issue is that the other jobs need not have monotone rank trajectories. Relative to a fixed rank rr, another job may therefore move into and out of relevance several times. SOAP decomposes the service received during these periods into relevant intervals. The quantity X0old​[r]X_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[r] denotes the service received in the job’s original relevant interval, while Xiold​[r]X_{i}^{\mathrm{old}}[r], i≥1i\geq 1, denotes the service received in its ii-th recycled relevant interval. Thus, even though the tagged job has been transformed to have a non-increasing rank trajectory, the non-monotonicity of the other jobs is retained through the collection {Xiold​[r]}i≥0\left\{X_{i}^{\mathrm{old}}[r]\right\}_{i\geq 0}. SOAP’s Vacation Transformation then represents the delays generated by these recycled relevant intervals in an equivalent transformed queue. Together with the worst-future-rank representation of the tagged job, this yields Proposition B.2.

There is one distinction from the non-increasing-rank case that is useful to keep in mind. When the original rank trajectory is non-increasing, the two terms in the expression of Proposition B.2 coincide with the physical waiting- and residence-time contributions defined in Section 2.2. For a general rank trajectory, however, the expression is obtained after the Worst Future Rank Substitution and Vacation Transformation, so we do not separately identify these two terms with the original job’s physical waiting and residence times. What these transformations preserve is their sum: the response time of the tagged job.

Finally, when a↦r⁡(d,a)a\mapsto r(d,a) is itself non-increasing for every descriptor dd, the worst rank is always equal to the current rank, so no worst-future-rank substitution is needed:

rd,xworst​(a)=r⁡(d,a).r_{d,x}^{\mathrm{worst}}(a)=r(d,a).

Moreover, another job can have at most one recycled relevant interval, so Xiold​[r]=0X_{i}^{\mathrm{old}}[r]=0 for all i≥2i\geq 2. The general SOAP identity therefore reduces exactly to Proposition 2.1.

Appendix C Proofs for Binary-Level Queues (Section 3)

This appendix supplies the deferred proofs from Section 3. Appendix C.1 proves Lemmas 3.1 and 3.2, and Appendix C.2 proves Lemma 3.4. Appendix C.3 proves the auxiliary cutoff comparison in Lemma C.1. Appendix C.4 proves the necessary workload and average-size bounds in Lemma 3.6; Appendix C.5 proves the tail-work estimate in Lemma 3.7. Throughout, Assumption 1 is in force.

C.1 Response-Time Identities (Lemmas 3.1 and 3.2)

Both identities follow by identifying the relevant old and new work in Proposition 2.1. Fixed ranks imply that there is no recycled old work. We give the full arguments for completeness.

Proof of Lemma 3.1.

Consider a tagged job with rank 00. We first analyze its waiting time. Since ranks are fixed, an old job cannot become irrelevant and later become relevant again. Hence there is no recycled old work, so Xiold​[0]=0X_{i}^{\mathrm{old}}[0]=0 for all i≥1i\geq 1, and in particular X1old​[0]=0X_{1}^{\mathrm{old}}[0]=0. An old job contributes relevant work precisely when it also has rank 00. Thus X0old[0]=S𝟏{Rρ=0}X_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[0]=S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=0\} and ρ0old​[0]=ρHIGH\rho_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[0]=\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}. Moreover, no future arrival can delay the tagged job: a future rank-00 job has the same rank but loses the FCFS tie, while a future rank-11 job has lower priority. Hence Xnew​[0]=0X^{\mathrm{new}}[0]=0 and ρnew​[0]=0\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[0]=0. Finally, the tagged job’s residence time is its own size as it cannot be preempted by future arrivals. Substituting these quantities into Proposition 2.1 and averaging over rank-00 jobs yields the lemma. ∎

Proof of Lemma 3.2.

Consider a tagged job with rank 11. We first analyze its waiting time. Since ranks are fixed, an old job cannot become irrelevant and later become relevant again, so Xiold​[1]=0X_{i}^{\mathrm{old}}[1]=0 for all i≥1i\geq 1. Every old job contributes relevant work: an old rank-00 job has higher priority, while an old rank-11 job has the same rank and wins the FCFS tie. Hence X0old​[1]=SX_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[1]=S and ρ0old​[1]=ρ\rho_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[1]=\rho. Among future arrivals, only rank-00 jobs can move ahead of the tagged job, so Xnew[1]=S𝟏{Rρ=0}X^{\mathrm{new}}[1]=S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=0\} and ρnew​[1]=ρHIGH\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[1]=\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}. During residence, the tagged job is interrupted only by future rank-00 work. Thus, for a rank-11 job of size xx, Proposition 2.1 gives the residence contribution ∫0xd​a1−ρnew​[1]=x1−ρHIGH\int_{0}^{x}\frac{da}{1-\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[1]}=\frac{x}{1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}}. Substituting these quantities into Proposition 2.1 and averaging over rank-11 jobs yields the lemma. ∎

C.2 Slack-Matched Size Cutoff (Lemma 3.4)

The lognormal-or-lighter regime means that H⁡(x)=Ω⁡((log⁡x)2)H(x)=\Omega((\log x)^{2}): for some κ>0\kappa>0, large jobs have tail probability at most e−κ​(log⁡x)2e^{-\kappa(\log x)^{2}}. To locate the slack-matched size cutoff within this regime, we use two auxiliary lemmas. The first compares it with the workload cutoff G−1​(ρ)G^{-1}(\rho); the second translates an integrated hazard bound into a bound on their logarithmic separation. Recall from Section 2 that G(x)=𝔼[S𝟏{S≤x}]/𝔼[S]G(x)=\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{S\leq x\}]/\mathbb{E}[S]. Thus G−1​(ρ)G^{-1}(\rho) leaves a 1−ρ1-\rho fraction of total work above the cutoff, whereas s¯ρ\bar{s}_{\rho} leaves a 1−ρ1-\rho fraction of jobs.

Lemma C.1 (Cutoff comparison).

In the lognormal-or-lighter regime, as ρ↑1\rho\uparrow 1 ,

H⁡(G−1​(ρ))−H⁡(s¯ρ)log⁡G−1​(ρ)⟶1.\frac{H(G^{-1}(\rho))-H(\bar{s}_{\rho})}{\log G^{-1}(\rho)}\longrightarrow 1.

We prove the lemma in Appendix C.3.

Lemma C.2 (Logarithmic integral).

For 1≤a≤b1\leq a\leq b with b>1b>1, let Δ=log⁡(b/a)\Delta=\log(b/a). Then

1log⁡b​∫ablog⁡uu​𝑑u=1log⁡b⋅Δ2​(log⁡b+log⁡a)=Δ−Δ22​log⁡b,\frac{1}{\log b}\int_{a}^{b}\frac{\log u}{u}\,du=\frac{1}{\log b}\cdot\frac{\Delta}{2}(\log b+\log a)=\Delta-\frac{\Delta^{2}}{2\log b},

and hence

Δ2≤1log⁡b​∫ablog⁡uu​𝑑u≤Δ.\frac{\Delta}{2}\leq\frac{1}{\log b}\int_{a}^{b}\frac{\log u}{u}\,du\leq\Delta.

∫ablog⁡uu​𝑑u=(log⁡b)2−(log⁡a)22=(log⁡b−log⁡a)​(log⁡b+log⁡a)2=Δ⁡(2​log⁡b−Δ)2.\int_{a}^{b}\frac{\log u}{u}\,du=\frac{(\log b)^{2}-(\log a)^{2}}{2}=\frac{(\log b-\log a)(\log b+\log a)}{2}=\frac{\Delta(2\log b-\Delta)}{2}.
