C.3 Cutoff Comparison (Lemma C.1)

Proof of Lemma C.1.

We compare two cutoffs associated with the fraction 1−ρ1-\rho: s¯ρ\bar{s}_{\rho} leaves that fraction of jobs above it, whereas G−1​(ρ)G^{-1}(\rho) leaves that fraction of total work above it.

By definition, G(x)=𝔼[S𝟏{S≤x}]/𝔼[S]G(x)=\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{S\leq x\}]/\mathbb{E}[S]. Thus G​(G−1​(ρ))=ρG(G^{-1}(\rho))=\rho implies 𝔼[S𝟏{S≤G−1(ρ)}]=ρ𝔼[S]\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{S\leq G^{-1}(\rho)\}]=\rho\mathbb{E}[S]. Subtracting this contribution from the mean work per arrival, 𝔼⁡[S]\mathbb{E}[S], gives the expected work per arrival contributed by jobs above the cutoff. Using F¯​(s¯ρ)=1−ρ\overline{F}(\bar{s}_{\rho})=1-\rho, we obtain

𝔼[S𝟏{S>G−1(ρ)}]=(1−ρ)𝔼[S]=F¯(s¯ρ)𝔼[S].\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{S>G^{-1}(\rho)\}]=(1-\rho)\mathbb{E}[S]=\overline{F}(\bar{s}_{\rho})\mathbb{E}[S].

Because the service distribution has unbounded support, its tail probability and tail work are positive at every finite threshold. Its mean is finite and positive by Lemma A.1, so both tail targets tend to zero as ρ↑1\rho\uparrow 1. Both cutoffs therefore tend to infinity.

A job with size exceeding G−1​(ρ)G^{-1}(\rho) contributes at least G−1​(ρ)G^{-1}(\rho) units of work. Consequently, the expected work per arrival contributed by these jobs is at least G−1​(ρ)G^{-1}(\rho) times the probability that an arrival exceeds this cutoff. Lemma A.4 bounds this expected work from above by twice the same quantity once ρ\rho is sufficiently close to one. Thus,

G−1​(ρ)​F¯​(G−1​(ρ))≤(1−ρ)​𝔼​[S]≤2​G−1​(ρ)​F¯​(G−1​(ρ)).G^{-1}(\rho)\overline{F}(G^{-1}(\rho))\leq(1-\rho)\mathbb{E}[S]\leq 2G^{-1}(\rho)\overline{F}(G^{-1}(\rho)).

Dividing by 𝔼​[S]​F¯​(G−1​(ρ))\mathbb{E}[S]\overline{F}(G^{-1}(\rho)) and substituting 1−ρ=F¯​(s¯ρ)1-\rho=\overline{F}(\bar{s}_{\rho}), we obtain

G−1​(ρ)𝔼⁡[S]≤F¯​(s¯ρ)F¯​(G−1​(ρ))≤2​G−1​(ρ)𝔼⁡[S].\frac{G^{-1}(\rho)}{\mathbb{E}[S]}\leq\frac{\overline{F}(\bar{s}_{\rho})}{\overline{F}(G^{-1}(\rho))}\leq\frac{2G^{-1}(\rho)}{\mathbb{E}[S]}.

Thus, the ratio of the tail probabilities lies within a factor of two of G−1​(ρ)/𝔼​[S]G^{-1}(\rho)/\mathbb{E}[S]. Taking logarithms converts this multiplicative comparison into an additive comparison of cumulative hazards. Since H=−log⁡F¯H=-\log\overline{F},

log⁡F¯​(s¯ρ)F¯​(G−1​(ρ))=H⁡(G−1​(ρ))−H⁡(s¯ρ).\log\frac{\overline{F}(\bar{s}_{\rho})}{\overline{F}(G^{-1}(\rho))}=H(G^{-1}(\rho))-H(\bar{s}_{\rho}).

Taking logarithms in the preceding bounds therefore gives

log⁡G−1​(ρ)−log⁡𝔼⁡[S]≤H⁡(G−1​(ρ))−H⁡(s¯ρ)≤log⁡G−1​(ρ)−log⁡𝔼⁡[S]+log⁡2.\log G^{-1}(\rho)-\log\mathbb{E}[S]\leq H(G^{-1}(\rho))-H(\bar{s}_{\rho})\leq\log G^{-1}(\rho)-\log\mathbb{E}[S]+\log 2.

Since G−1​(ρ)→∞G^{-1}(\rho)\to\infty and 𝔼⁡[S]\mathbb{E}[S] is a fixed positive constant, the lower bound is eventually positive. Monotonicity of HH then gives s¯ρ<G−1​(ρ)\bar{s}_{\rho}<G^{-1}(\rho). Finally, dividing both bounds by log⁡G−1​(ρ)→∞\log G^{-1}(\rho)\to\infty makes the additive constants vanish, yielding

H⁡(G−1​(ρ))−H⁡(s¯ρ)log⁡G−1​(ρ)⟶1.\frac{H(G^{-1}(\rho))-H(\bar{s}_{\rho})}{\log G^{-1}(\rho)}\longrightarrow 1.

∎

C.4 Necessary Workload and Average-Size Bounds (Lemma 3.6)

Proof of Lemma 3.6.

Suppose that a BLQ policy φρ\varphi_{\rho} is heavy-traffic order-optimal along a sequence ρ↑1\rho\uparrow 1. All limits and order bounds in this proof are taken along that sequence. For some finite C>0C>0,

𝔼⁡[Tφρ]≤C(1−ρ)​G−1​(ρ).\mathbb{E}[T^{\varphi_{\rho}}]\leq\frac{C}{(1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho)}.

Recall that the high-priority slack equals the original system slack plus the load carried by demoted jobs:

1−ρHIGH=(1−ρ)+λρ𝔼[S𝟏{Rρ=1}].1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}=(1-\rho)+\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=1\}].

We first show that only a small fraction of jobs can be demoted, then that these jobs must nevertheless carry substantial work. Together, the two requirements force the average low-priority job size to be large.

Low-priority delay limits the fraction of demoted jobs.

The waiting term in Lemma 3.2 is already a lower bound on the overall mean response time. Comparing it with the assumed upper bound gives

ℙ⁡(Rρ=1)​λρ​𝔼​[S2]2​(1−ρ)​(1−ρHIGH)≤𝔼⁡[Tφρ]≤C(1−ρ)​G−1​(ρ).\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}=1)\frac{\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[S^{2}]}{2(1-\rho)(1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}})}\leq\mathbb{E}[T^{\varphi_{\rho}}]\leq\frac{C}{(1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho)}.

Cancelling the common factor 1/(1−ρ)1/(1-\rho), and using λρ→1/𝔼⁡[S]>0\lambda_{\rho}\to 1/\mathbb{E}[S]>0, yields

ℙ⁡(Rρ=1)​G−1​(ρ)=O⁡(1−ρHIGH).\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}=1)G^{-1}(\rho)=O\!\left(1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}\right). (11)

Because 1−ρHIGH≤11-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}\leq 1 and G−1​(ρ)→∞G^{-1}(\rho)\to\infty, we obtain

ℙ⁡(Rρ=1)=O⁡(1G−1​(ρ))=o⁡(1).\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}=1)=O\!\left(\frac{1}{G^{-1}(\rho)}\right)=o(1).

Thus low-priority waiting would be too costly if a nonvanishing fraction of arrivals incurred it.

High-priority delay requires substantial work to be demoted.

A vanishing low-priority fraction leaves essentially all second-moment mass at high priority. This claim needs justification because the demoted jobs may be precisely the largest ones. For any fixed K>0K>0, splitting the demoted jobs’ second-moment contribution at size KK gives

𝔼[S2𝟏{Rρ=1}]≤K2ℙ(Rρ=1)+𝔼[S2𝟏{S>K}].\mathbb{E}[S^{2}\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=1\}]\leq K^{2}\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}=1)+\mathbb{E}[S^{2}\mathbf{1}\{S>K\}].

The first term vanishes as ρ↑1\rho\uparrow 1; the second can be made arbitrarily small by taking KK large, since 𝔼⁡[S2]<∞\mathbb{E}[S^{2}]<\infty by Lemma A.1 . This argument applies to every measurable, load-dependent assignment map, including randomized maps. It does not require the sets of demoted jobs to converge as ρ\rho changes.

It follows that 𝔼[S2𝟏{Rρ=0}]→𝔼[S2]>0\mathbb{E}[S^{2}\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=0\}]\to\mathbb{E}[S^{2}]>0, while ℙ⁡(Rρ=0)→1\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}=0)\to 1. The high-priority waiting contribution in Lemma 3.1 therefore gives, for some c>0c>0 and all sufficiently large ρ\rho,

c1−ρHIGH≤𝔼⁡[Tφρ]≤C(1−ρ)​G−1​(ρ).\frac{c}{1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}}\leq\mathbb{E}[T^{\varphi_{\rho}}]\leq\frac{C}{(1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho)}.

Consequently,

1−ρHIGH=Ω⁡((1−ρ)​G−1​(ρ)).1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}=\Omega\!\left((1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho)\right). (12)

This required slack is much larger than the original slack 1−ρ1-\rho, because G−1​(ρ)→∞G^{-1}(\rho)\to\infty. The slack identity at the start of the proof shows that demotion is the only source of the increase. Subtracting the negligible 1−ρ1-\rho term and using λρ=Θ⁡(1)\lambda_{\rho}=\Theta(1) gives

𝔼[S𝟏{Rρ=1}]=Ω((1−ρ)G−1(ρ)).\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=1\}]=\Omega\!\left((1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho)\right). (13)

A small fraction carrying substantial work must be large on average.

The preceding work bound makes the original slack 1−ρ1-\rho negligible compared with the work demoted per arrival. The slack identity and λρ=Θ⁡(1)\lambda_{\rho}=\Theta(1) therefore give

1−ρHIGH=Θ(𝔼[S𝟏{Rρ=1}]).1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}=\Theta\!\left(\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=1\}]\right).

Substituting into (11) yields

ℙ(Rρ=1)G−1(ρ)=O(𝔼[S𝟏{Rρ=1}]).\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}=1)G^{-1}(\rho)=O\!\left(\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=1\}]\right).

Moreover, (13) ensures that the expected demoted work is positive for all sufficiently large ρ\rho, and hence ℙ⁡(Rρ=1)>0\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}=1)>0. We may therefore divide by the demotion probability to obtain

𝔼⁡[S∣Rρ=1]=𝔼[S𝟏{Rρ=1}]ℙ⁡(Rρ=1)=Ω⁡(G−1​(ρ)).\mathbb{E}[S\mid R_{\rho}=1]=\frac{\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}=1\}]}{\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}=1)}=\Omega(G^{-1}(\rho)).

Together with (13), this proves both requirements in the lemma. The argument explains their joint role: removing enough work protects the high-priority queue, while selecting only a few large jobs limits the low-priority contribution to the overall mean. ∎

C.5 Tail-Work Scarcity (Lemma 3.7)

Lemma 3.6 gives the work that an order-optimal BLQ policy must demote. We now show that, in the intermediate regime, even all jobs above any fixed positive multiple of G−1​(ρ)G^{-1}(\rho) cannot supply this amount. We use the tail-work bound from Lemma A.3 in Appendix A.3.

Proof of Lemma 3.7.

Fix d>0d>0. At the threshold G−1​(ρ)G^{-1}(\rho), the total tail work is exactly (1−ρ)​𝔼​[S](1-\rho)\mathbb{E}[S], a factor of order G−1​(ρ)G^{-1}(\rho) smaller than the work required by Lemma 3.6. If d≥1d\geq 1, raising the threshold can only reduce the available work, so

𝔼[S𝟏{S>dG−1(ρ)}](1−ρ)​G−1​(ρ)≤𝔼⁡[S]G−1​(ρ)⟶0.\frac{\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{S>dG^{-1}(\rho)\}]}{(1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho)}\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}[S]}{G^{-1}(\rho)}\longrightarrow 0.

The issue is therefore whether lowering the threshold by a fixed factor d<1d<1 could supply enough additional work to close this gap.

Suppose 0<d<10<d<1. In the intermediate regime, Lemma A.2 gives u​h​(u)/log⁡u→0uh(u)/\log u\to 0. For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, we thus have h⁡(u)≤ε​log⁡u/uh(u)\leq\varepsilon\log u/u throughout [d​x,x][dx,x] for all sufficiently large xx. Integrating gives

0≤H⁡(x)−H⁡(d​x)≤ε⁡(log⁡(1/d)​log​x−(log⁡d)22).0\leq H(x)-H(dx)\leq\varepsilon\left(\log(1/d)\log x-\frac{(\log d)^{2}}{2}\right).

After division by log⁡x\log x, the upper bound can be made arbitrarily small by choosing ε\varepsilon. Hence H⁡(x)−H⁡(d​x)=o⁡(log⁡x)H(x)-H(dx)=o(\log x), or equivalently,

F¯​(d​x)F¯​(x)=eH⁡(x)−H⁡(d​x)=xo⁡(1).\frac{\overline{F}(dx)}{\overline{F}(x)}=e^{H(x)-H(dx)}=x^{o(1)}. (14)

Thus a fixed proportional reduction of the threshold increases the tail probability by less than any fixed positive power of xx. It cannot produce the factor of order xx needed to meet the low-priority work requirement. To transfer this probability comparison to work, Lemma A.3 gives a constant Cd<∞C_{d}<\infty such that, eventually,

𝔼[S𝟏{S>dG−1(ρ)}]≤CdG−1(ρ)F¯(dG−1(ρ))\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{S>dG^{-1}(\rho)\}]\leq C_{d}G^{-1}(\rho)\overline{F}(dG^{-1}(\rho)) =Cd​G−1​(ρ)​F¯​(G−1​(ρ))​(G−1​(ρ))o⁡(1)\displaystyle=C_{d}G^{-1}(\rho)\overline{F}(G^{-1}(\rho))\bigl(G^{-1}(\rho)\bigr)^{o(1)}
≤Cd​(1−ρ)​𝔼​[S]​(G−1​(ρ))o⁡(1).\displaystyle\leq C_{d}(1-\rho)\mathbb{E}[S]\bigl(G^{-1}(\rho)\bigr)^{o(1)}.

The last inequality uses G−1(ρ)F¯(G−1(ρ))≤𝔼[S𝟏{S>G−1(ρ)}]=(1−ρ)𝔼[S]G^{-1}(\rho)\overline{F}(G^{-1}(\rho))\leq\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{S>G^{-1}(\rho)\}]=(1-\rho)\mathbb{E}[S]. Dividing by the required work scale yields

𝔼[S𝟏{S>dG−1(ρ)}](1−ρ)​G−1​(ρ)≤Cd​𝔼​[S]​(G−1​(ρ))−1+o⁡(1)⟶0.\frac{\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{S>dG^{-1}(\rho)\}]}{(1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho)}\leq C_{d}\mathbb{E}[S]\bigl(G^{-1}(\rho)\bigr)^{-1+o(1)}\longrightarrow 0.

This is the desired scarcity bound. Even assigning every job above d​G−1​(ρ)dG^{-1}(\rho) to low priority cannot supply the amount of work demanded by an order-optimal BLQ policy. ∎

Appendix D Sparse Predict and Demote (Section 4)

Throughout this appendix, Assumption 1 holds and the service distribution is in the lognormal-or-lighter regime. The exact-prediction arguments fix θ∈(0,θ¯)\theta\in(0,\bar{\theta}) and use bρ​(θ)=θ​G−1​(ρ)b_{\rho}(\theta)=\theta G^{-1}(\rho) and the feasible trigger interval from Section 4.2.

D.1 Abundance of Jobs above Residual Barrier (Lemma 4.2)

Proof of Lemma 4.2.

The fraction of jobs above the residual barrier is F¯​(θ​G−1​(ρ))\overline{F}(\theta G^{-1}(\rho)), while the desired demotion fraction is 1−ρ=F¯​(s¯ρ)1-\rho=\overline{F}(\bar{s}_{\rho}). Because F¯​(u)=e−H⁡(u)\overline{F}(u)=e^{-H(u)}, the logarithm of this ratio is H⁡(s¯ρ)−H⁡(θ​G−1​(ρ))H(\bar{s}_{\rho})-H(\theta G^{-1}(\rho)). In words, the hazard accumulated between the cutoffs measures how much the survival probability decreases when the cutoff is raised. If this hazard increment diverges, lowering the cutoff increases the fraction of jobs above residual barrier by an unbounded factor. We show that even a fixed proportional part of this interval contributes a diverging hazard increment.

Choose θ~∈(θ,θ¯)\widetilde{\theta}\in(\theta,\bar{\theta}). Since s¯ρ/G−1​(ρ)→θ¯\bar{s}_{\rho}/G^{-1}(\rho)\to\bar{\theta}, eventually s¯ρ≥θ~​G−1​(ρ)\bar{s}_{\rho}\geq\widetilde{\theta}G^{-1}(\rho). By Lemma A.2, u​h​(u)/log⁡uuh(u)/\log u has a positive or infinite limit. Thus there is a fixed c>0c>0 such that h⁡(u)≥c​log⁡u/uh(u)\geq c\log u/u for all sufficiently large uu. As θ​G−1​(ρ)→∞\theta G^{-1}(\rho)\to\infty, this bound holds throughout the interval below, giving

The last inequality uses log⁡u≥log⁡(θ​G−1​(ρ))\log u\geq\log(\theta G^{-1}(\rho)) throughout the integration interval. Since θ~/θ>1\widetilde{\theta}/\theta>1 is fixed, the lower bound diverges. In particular, the θ\theta-tuned query probability qρ​(θ)=(1−ρ)/F¯​(θ​G−1​(ρ))q_{\rho}(\theta)=(1-\rho)/\overline{F}(\theta G^{-1}(\rho)) , the reciprocal of this ratio, tends to zero. ∎

D.2 Response-Time Guarantee (Theorem 4.6)

For a positive trigger, an eventually demoted job’s rank rises from zero to one at age τ\tau. Thus Proposition 2.1, which requires ranks to be non-increasing in attained service, does not apply to this policy. We instead use the general SOAP identity in Proposition B.2. For intuition on its worst-future-rank construction, see Appendix B.2 and [28, Appendix D].

Recall that Rρ(θ,τ)=Qρ(θ,τ)𝟏{S>τ+bρ(θ)}R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=Q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)\mathbf{1}\{S>\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta)\} records eventual demotion. If Rρ​(θ,τ)=0R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=0 , the job is never demoted and receives all its service at high priority. If Rρ​(θ,τ)=1R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=1 , the job receives its first τ\tau units at high priority and is then demoted while still unfinished. The following analogues of Lemmas 3.1 and 3.2 condition on these two eventual outcomes; their derivations are given in Appendix D.3.

Lemma D.1 (Never demoted jobs).

For SPD⁡(bρ​(θ),qρ​(θ,τ),τ)\mathrm{SPD}(b_{\rho}(\theta),q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau),\tau) with τ∈[0,τ¯ρ​(θ)]\tau\in[0,\bar{\tau}_{\rho}(\theta)] ,

𝔼⁡[TSPD⁡(bρ​(θ),qρ​(θ,τ),τ)∣Rρ​(θ,τ)=0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[T^{\mathrm{SPD}(b_{\rho}(\theta),q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau),\tau)}\mid R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=0\right]
=λρ𝔼[(min{S,τ}+max{0,S−τ}𝟏{Rρ(θ,τ)=0})2]2​(1−ρρHIGH​(θ,τ))+𝔼⁡[S∣Rρ​(θ,τ)=0].\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left(\min\{S,\tau\}+\max\{0,S-\tau\}\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=0\}\right)^{2}\right]}{2(1-\rho_{\rho}^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\theta,\tau))}+\mathbb{E}[S\mid R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=0].
Lemma D.2 (Eventually demoted jobs).

For SPD⁡(bρ​(θ),qρ​(θ,τ),τ)\mathrm{SPD}(b_{\rho}(\theta),q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau),\tau) with τ∈[0,τ¯ρ​(θ)]\tau\in[0,\bar{\tau}_{\rho}(\theta)] ,

𝔼⁡[TSPD⁡(bρ​(θ),qρ​(θ,τ),τ)∣Rρ​(θ,τ)=1]=λρ​𝔼​[S2]2​(1−ρ)​(1−ρρHIGH​(θ,τ))+𝔼⁡[S∣Rρ​(θ,τ)=1]1−ρρHIGH​(θ,τ).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[T^{\mathrm{SPD}(b_{\rho}(\theta),q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau),\tau)}\mid R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=1\right]=\frac{\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[S^{2}]}{2(1-\rho)(1-\rho_{\rho}^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\theta,\tau))}+\frac{\mathbb{E}[S\mid R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=1]}{1-\rho_{\rho}^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\theta,\tau)}.

In each lemma, the first summand is a SOAP waiting contribution and the second is a SOAP residence contribution. For a never-demoted tagged job, its worst future rank equals its actual rank zero, so these are its expected physical waiting and service times. For an eventually demoted tagged job, SOAP instead assigns rank one throughout. This preserves response time, but the separate contributions need not equal its original physical waiting and residence times.

Proof of Theorem 4.6.

Lemma 4.4 establishes that the ex-ante query probability vanishes uniformly. It remains to prove the response-time bound. We combine the two conditional formulas in Lemmas D.1 and D.2, weighting them by the probabilities of the eventual outcomes ℙ⁡(Rρ​(θ,τ)=0)=ρ\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=0)=\rho and ℙ⁡(Rρ​(θ,τ)=1)=1−ρ\mathbb{P}(R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=1)=1-\rho. Lemma 4.5 gives these probabilities directly. Lemma A.1 in Appendix A.1 ensures that 𝔼⁡[S]\mathbb{E}[S] and 𝔼⁡[S2]\mathbb{E}[S^{2}] are finite constants, with 𝔼⁡[S]>0\mathbb{E}[S]>0; hence λρ=ρ/𝔼⁡[S]→1/𝔼⁡[S]\lambda_{\rho}=\rho/\mathbb{E}[S]\to 1/\mathbb{E}[S]. We first bound the entire contribution of jobs that are never demoted. Their probability is ρ≤1\rho\leq 1, and the high-priority service generated by any competing arrival is at most SS. Applying Lemma D.1 therefore gives

𝔼[TSPD⁡(bρ​(θ),qρ​(θ,τ),τ)𝟏{Rρ(θ,τ)=0}]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[T^{\mathrm{SPD}(b_{\rho}(\theta),q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau),\tau)}\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=0\}\right] ≤λρ​𝔼​[S2]2​(1−ρρHIGH​(θ,τ))+𝔼[S𝟏{Rρ(θ,τ)=0}]\displaystyle\leq\frac{\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[S^{2}]}{2(1-\rho_{\rho}^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\theta,\tau))}+\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=0\}]
=O⁡(1(1−ρ)​G−1​(ρ))+O⁡(1).\displaystyle=O\!\left(\frac{1}{(1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho)}\right)+O(1).

Here Lemma 4.5 bounds the waiting term uniformly in τ\tau, and the residence term is at most 𝔼⁡[S]\mathbb{E}[S].

Next consider eventually demoted jobs. Multiplying Lemma D.2 by the demotion probability 1−ρ1-\rho cancels the extra factor 1−ρ1-\rho in the waiting denominator and gives

𝔼[TSPD⁡(bρ​(θ),qρ​(θ,τ),τ)𝟏{Rρ(θ,τ)=1}]=λρ​𝔼​[S2]2​(1−ρρHIGH​(θ,τ))+𝔼[S𝟏{Rρ(θ,τ)=1}]1−ρρHIGH​(θ,τ).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[T^{\mathrm{SPD}(b_{\rho}(\theta),q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau),\tau)}\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=1\}\right]=\frac{\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[S^{2}]}{2(1-\rho_{\rho}^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\theta,\tau))}+\frac{\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=1\}]}{1-\rho_{\rho}^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\theta,\tau)}.

The first term has the same uniform bound as above. Although the conditional mean 𝔼⁡[S∣Rρ​(θ,τ)=1]\mathbb{E}[S\mid R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=1] may grow, weighting by the demotion probability gives 𝔼[S𝟏{Rρ(θ,τ)=1}]≤𝔼[S]\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=1\}]\leq\mathbb{E}[S]. As a result, the residence term is also bounded uniformly over feasible triggers by

𝔼[S𝟏{Rρ(θ,τ)=1}]1−ρρHIGH​(θ,τ)≤𝔼⁡[S]1−ρρHIGH​(θ,τ)=O⁡(1(1−ρ)​G−1​(ρ)),\frac{\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=1\}]}{1-\rho_{\rho}^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\theta,\tau)}\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}[S]}{1-\rho_{\rho}^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\theta,\tau)}=O\!\left(\frac{1}{(1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho)}\right),

The remaining O⁡(1)O(1) term is negligible on this scale: by finite second moment,

(1−ρ)​G−1​(ρ)=G−1(ρ)𝔼[S𝟏{S>G−1(ρ)}]𝔼⁡[S]≤𝔼[S2𝟏{S>G−1(ρ)}]𝔼⁡[S]⟶0.(1-\rho)G^{-1}(\rho)=\frac{G^{-1}(\rho)\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{S>G^{-1}(\rho)\}]}{\mathbb{E}[S]}\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}[S^{2}\mathbf{1}\{S>G^{-1}(\rho)\}]}{\mathbb{E}[S]}\longrightarrow 0.

Summing the weighted waiting and residence contributions gives

uniformly over the feasible trigger interval. SRPT optimality and the benchmark (2) give the matching lower bound for every trigger. This proves uniform heavy-traffic order-optimality and completes the theorem. ∎

D.3 Proofs of Auxiliary Lemmas (Lemmas D.1 and D.2)

We now prove Lemmas D.1 and D.2. As explained above, the rank increase at a positive trigger requires Proposition B.2; the following rank representation supplies its inputs. Fix ρ\rho and a feasible trigger τ\tau. Recall that Qρ​(θ,τ)Q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau) is the Bernoulli selection coin used by the policy at the trigger. The policy queries an unfinished job at the trigger with the (θ,τ)(\theta,\tau)-tuned query probability qρ​(θ,τ)q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau) without using job size, so this coin has that Bernoulli law independently of SS. For analysis, we may generate it at arrival and use it only if the job reaches the trigger; this gives exactly the same policy. Recall that Rρ(θ,τ)=Qρ(θ,τ)𝟏{S>τ+bρ(θ)}R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=Q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)\mathbf{1}\{S>\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta)\} is the eventual demotion indicator. Using the job’s size and eventual demotion indicator as its SOAP descriptor, its rank at attained service age aa is

r((S,Rρ(θ,τ)),a)=Rρ(θ,τ)𝟏{a≥τ},0≤a<S.r((S,R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)),a)=R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)\mathbf{1}\{a\geq\tau\},\qquad 0\leq a<S.

The descriptor encodes the eventual demotion decision for analysis. Before the trigger, its rank is zero regardless of the hidden size or sampling outcome; the scheduler still queries only selected jobs that remain unfinished at that age.

The FCFS rule uses original arrival time in both queues. Older jobs win equal-rank ties, whereas future arrivals lose them. Thus old-job relevant service includes ranks at most the tagged rank, and new-job relevant service includes only ranks strictly smaller. A competitor’s rank can only increase, so it cannot reenter relevance after leaving: Xiold​[r]=0X_{i}^{\mathrm{old}}[r]=0 for i≥1i\geq 1 and r∈{0,1}r\in\{0,1\}. The service variables below describe the relevant service generated by a generic arrival, not its remaining service at an observation time. The corresponding load is the arrival rate λρ\lambda_{\rho} multiplied by the mean of that relevant-service variable.

Proof of Lemma D.1.

A tagged job that is never demoted has rank zero until completion, so its worst future rank is also zero. An older job delays it only during that older job’s high-priority service: service until completion or age τ\tau, whichever comes first, together with any remaining service if the older job is never demoted. Therefore

X0old​[0]\displaystyle X_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[0] =min{S,τ}+max{0,S−τ}𝟏{Rρ(θ,τ)=0},\displaystyle=\min\{S,\tau\}+\max\{0,S-\tau\}\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=0\},
ρ0old​[0]\displaystyle\rho_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[0] =λρ​𝔼​[X0old​[0]]=ρρHIGH​(θ,τ).\displaystyle=\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[X_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[0]]=\rho_{\rho}^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\theta,\tau).

The last equality follows from the definition of ρρHIGH​(θ,τ)\rho_{\rho}^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\theta,\tau) in Section 4.2: X0old​[0]X_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[0] is exactly the high-priority service generated by a generic arrival.

No future arrival can overtake the tagged job: even another rank-zero job loses the FCFS tie. Hence Xnew​[0]=0X^{\mathrm{new}}[0]=0 and ρnew​[0]=λρ​𝔼​[Xnew​[0]]=0\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[0]=\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[X^{\mathrm{new}}[0]]=0. The tagged job’s residence contribution is consequently its size. In Proposition B.2, the recycled relevant-work variables are zero, so the waiting numerator is λρ​𝔼​[(X0old​[0])2]\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[(X_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[0])^{2}]. The two slack factors are 1−ρρHIGH​(θ,τ)1-\rho_{\rho}^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\theta,\tau) and 1−ρnew​[0]=11-\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[0]=1. Thus a tagged job of size xx has the waiting term in the lemma plus residence xx. Taking expectation with respect to the conditional distribution of the tagged size given Rρ​(θ,τ)=0R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=0 replaces xx by 𝔼⁡[S∣Rρ​(θ,τ)=0]\mathbb{E}[S\mid R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=0]; the waiting term is unchanged. This proves the stated conditional response-time formula. Jobs finishing before the trigger are included automatically: they have Rρ​(θ,τ)=0R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=0 and receive their entire service at high priority. ∎

Proof of Lemma D.2.

An eventually demoted tagged job has worst future rank one at every age, including during its initial high-priority service. SOAP substitutes this worst future rank for the tagged job’s actual rank while preserving its response time. Competitors retain their original rank functions of attained service; see Appendix B.2 and [28, Appendix D].

An older competing job has rank zero or one throughout its service and wins ties at rank one. Hence all of its SS units of service are relevant to the rank-one tag, giving X0old​[1]=SX_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[1]=S and ρ0old​[1]=λρ​𝔼​[X0old​[1]]=λρ​𝔼​[S]=ρ\rho_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[1]=\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[X_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[1]]=\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[S]=\rho. A future arrival loses ties at rank one, so only its rank-zero service is relevant to this tag. This is the same high-priority work as X0old​[0]X_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[0], giving

Xnew​[1]\displaystyle X^{\mathrm{new}}[1] =X0old[0]=min{S,τ}+max{0,S−τ}𝟏{Rρ(θ,τ)=0},\displaystyle=X_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[0]=\min\{S,\tau\}+\max\{0,S-\tau\}\mathbf{1}\{R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=0\},
ρnew​[1]\displaystyle\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[1] =λρ​𝔼​[Xnew​[1]]=ρρHIGH​(θ,τ).\displaystyle=\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[X^{\mathrm{new}}[1]]=\rho_{\rho}^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\theta,\tau).

Since X0old​[1]=SX_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[1]=S and no recycled work contributes, the waiting numerator in Proposition B.2 is λρ​𝔼​[S2]\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[S^{2}]. These inputs give the two slack factors in the waiting term of Proposition B.2: 1−ρ1-\rho for all older work and 1−ρρHIGH​(θ,τ)1-\rho_{\rho}^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\theta,\tau) for high-priority work from future arrivals. The same new-arrival load ρnew​[1]=ρρHIGH​(θ,τ)\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[1]=\rho_{\rho}^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\theta,\tau) also enters the residence denominator. Since the substituted rank is constant, the residence integral for a tagged job of size xx is

∫0xd​a1−ρρHIGH​(θ,τ)=x1−ρρHIGH​(θ,τ).\int_{0}^{x}\frac{da}{1-\rho_{\rho}^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\theta,\tau)}=\frac{x}{1-\rho_{\rho}^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\theta,\tau)}.

Taking expectation with respect to the conditional distribution of the tagged size given Rρ​(θ,τ)=1R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=1 replaces xx in the residence term by 𝔼⁡[S∣Rρ​(θ,τ)=1]\mathbb{E}[S\mid R_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=1] ; the waiting term is unchanged. This proves the stated conditional response-time formula. The second moment 𝔼⁡[S2]\mathbb{E}[S^{2}] remains unconditional because it concerns competing arrivals, whose sizes are independent of the tagged job’s eventual demotion outcome. ∎

Appendix E Proofs for the Costly-Prediction Extension (Section 5.1)

Throughout this appendix, Assumption 1 holds. Appendix E.1 proves the free-to-costly comparison in Lemma 5.1 by combining response-time identities with bounds on inference work and slack. Appendix E.2 proves the supporting lemmas. The response-time identities allow general prediction rules applied independently across jobs.

The remaining subsections study how trigger choice affects query use and inference load under exact predictions. Appendix E.3 establishes cutoff estimates and feasibility of proportional triggers. Appendices E.4–E.6 use these tools to give detailed proofs of the results in Proposition 5.4 for polylogarithmic, rapidly varying, and regularly varying cumulative hazards, respectively. Appendices E.3–E.6 additionally assume that the service distribution is in the lognormal-or-lighter regime.

E.1 Reduction from Free to Costly Predictions (Lemma 5.1)

Fix ρ<1\rho<1, a deterministic trigger τ≥0\tau\geq 0, and an inference duration δ≥0\delta\geq 0, and suppress load subscripts. Let π\pi denote the policy with these fixed parameters and FCFS in both queues. Recall that QqryQ^{\mathrm{qry}} is the actual-query indicator from Section 4.2 and RR for the eventual-demotion indicator, with R≤Qqry≤𝟏{S>τ}R\leq Q^{\mathrm{qry}}\leq\mathbf{1}\{S>\tau\}, so every demoted job has been queried. The triples (S,Qqry,R)(S,Q^{\mathrm{qry}},R) are i.i.d. across jobs and independent of Poisson arrivals of rate λ\lambda. Their components within a job may be dependent. Recall that inference work is done while the job is still in the high-priority queue and consumes server capacity. During this time, ordinary-service age is paused, and both queues break ties by original arrival time.

Total work per arrival is S+δ​QqryS+\delta Q^{\mathrm{qry}}, and the work sent to low priority is (S−τ)​R(S-\tau)R. We define

ρ⁡(δ):=λ​𝔼​[S+δ​Qqry],ρHIGH​(δ):=λ​𝔼​[S+δ​Qqry−(S−τ)​R].\rho(\delta):=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S+\delta Q^{\mathrm{qry}}],\qquad\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\delta):=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S+\delta Q^{\mathrm{qry}}-(S-\tau)R].

as the corresponding loads (including inference) for the total system and the high-priority queue respectively. The free-policy loads are ρ⁡(0)=ρ\rho(0)=\rho and ρHIGH​(0)\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(0).

We separate the response-time identity into two lemmas, one for each eventual demotion outcome, and then state bounds on inference duration, slack, and second moments. These four lemmas reduce the proof of Lemma 5.1 to a comparison of the SOAP terms. Their proofs follow in Appendix E.2.

If ρ⁡(δ)<1\rho(\delta)<1, then

𝔼⁡[Tπ​(δ)​(1−R)]=ℙ⁡(R=0)​λ​𝔼​[(S+δ​Qqry−(S−τ)​R)2]2​(1−ρHIGH​(δ))+𝔼⁡[(S+δ​Qqry)​(1−R)].\mathbb{E}[T^{\pi}(\delta)(1-R)]=\frac{\mathbb{P}(R=0)\lambda\mathbb{E}[(S+\delta Q^{\mathrm{qry}}-(S-\tau)R)^{2}]}{2(1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\delta))}+\mathbb{E}[(S+\delta Q^{\mathrm{qry}})(1-R)].

Fix ρ∈[1/2,1)\rho\in[1/2,1) and a SPD policy π\pi satisfying the slack-preservation condition (7). Compare its free and costly versions with the same policy parameters and prediction law, so (S,Qqry,R)(S,Q^{\mathrm{qry}},R) has the same distribution in both.

Comparison of the Four SOAP Terms. We apply Lemmas E.1 and E.2 at δ\delta and at 00. The common law of (S,Qqry,R)(S,Q^{\mathrm{qry}},R) keeps each group’s probability weight unchanged when inference is added. We compare waiting and residence for each group.

Never-demoted waiting.

We start by focusing on the first term in Lemma E.1, the probability-weighted waiting contribution of never-demoted jobs. E.2 Proofs of Auxiliary Lemmas (Lemmas E.1–E.4)

Proof of Lemma E.1.

SOAP age includes inference work, and all recycled relevant-work terms vanish because ranks never decrease. As in the proof of Lemma D.1, a never-demoted tagged job has worst future rank zero. Older arrivals contribute high-priority work, now including inference, while future arrivals lose the FCFS tie. Thus the SOAP inputs are66 6 Here ρ⁡(0)\rho(0) is the total load when δ=0\delta=0, whereas ρ0old​[0]=λ​𝔼​[X0old​[0]]\rho_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[0]=\lambda\mathbb{E}[X_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[0]] is the SOAP load from original, non-recycled old work relevant to rank zero. The subscript and bracketed argument in the latter notation do not specify the inference cost.

X0old​[0]\displaystyle X_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[0] =S+δ​Qqry−(S−τ)​R,\displaystyle=S+\delta Q^{\mathrm{qry}}-(S-\tau)R, ρ0old​[0]\displaystyle\rho_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[0] =ρHIGH​(δ),\displaystyle=\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\delta),
Xnew​[0]\displaystyle X^{\mathrm{new}}[0] =0,\displaystyle=0, ρnew​[0]\displaystyle\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[0] =0.\displaystyle=0.

The tagged job’s own work is S+δ​QqryS+\delta Q^{\mathrm{qry}}. Substituting these inputs into Proposition B.2, averaging over the tagged-job distribution conditional on R=0R=0, and multiplying by ℙ⁡(R=0)\mathbb{P}(R=0) proves Lemma E.1. ∎

Proof of Lemma E.2.

As in the proof of Lemma D.2, an eventually demoted tagged job has worst future rank one throughout. Older arrivals contribute total work, while future arrivals contribute only high-priority work. Including inference gives

X0old​[1]\displaystyle X_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[1] =S+δ​Qqry,\displaystyle=S+\delta Q^{\mathrm{qry}}, ρ0old​[1]\displaystyle\rho_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[1] =ρ⁡(δ),\displaystyle=\rho(\delta),
Xnew​[1]\displaystyle X^{\mathrm{new}}[1] =S+δ​Qqry−(S−τ)​R,\displaystyle=S+\delta Q^{\mathrm{qry}}-(S-\tau)R, ρnew​[1]\displaystyle\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[1] =ρHIGH​(δ).\displaystyle=\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\delta).

All older work remains relevant to a rank-one tagged job until completion, so Xiold​[1]=0X_{i}^{\mathrm{old}}[1]=0 for every i≥1i\geq 1. These loads give the two waiting denominators. Since the tagged job’s worst future rank is constant, its residence contribution is (S+δ​Qqry)/(1−ρHIGH​(δ))(S+\delta Q^{\mathrm{qry}})/(1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\delta)). Applying Proposition B.2, average conditional on R=1R=1 and multiplying by ℙ⁡(R=1)\mathbb{P}(R=1), weobtain the identity in Lemma E.2. ∎

E.3 Tools for Distribution-Specific Comparisons

Throughout Appendices E.4–E.6, we fix θ∈(0,θ¯)\theta\in(0,\bar{\theta}), use exact predictions with residual barrier bρ​(θ)=θ​G−1​(ρ)b_{\rho}(\theta)=\theta G^{-1}(\rho), and use the γ\gamma-exponential cost scale (8) with fixed γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1). The tail assumptions describe HH at multiples of the workload cutoff G−1​(ρ)G^{-1}(\rho), whereas the stability criterion in Lemma 5.3 uses H⁡(s¯ρ)H(\bar{s}_{\rho}). The first lemma shows that H⁡(s¯ρ)H(\bar{s}_{\rho}) and H​(G−1​(ρ))H(G^{-1}(\rho)) are asymptotically equal, allowing us to apply the tail assumptions in that criterion. The second establishes feasibility of fixed proportional triggers at sufficiently high loads.

Lemma E.5 (Cutoff scales).

As ρ↑1\rho\uparrow 1, the ratio of cumulative hazard for s¯ρ\bar{s}_{\rho} and G−1​(ρ)G^{-1}(\rho) goes to 11:

H⁡(s¯ρ)H​(G−1​(ρ))⟶1.\frac{H(\bar{s}_{\rho})}{H(G^{-1}(\rho))}\longrightarrow 1.
Proof of Lemma E.5.

By the definition of the workload distribution GG, the sizes above G−1​(ρ)G^{-1}(\rho) contribute a 1−ρ1-\rho fraction of the total workload. This gives the first equality below; Lemma A.4 gives the second:

(1−ρ)𝔼[S]=𝔼[S𝟏{S>G−1(ρ)}]=G−1(ρ)F¯(G−1(ρ))(1+o(1)).(1-\rho)\mathbb{E}[S]=\mathbb{E}[S\mathbf{1}\{S>G^{-1}(\rho)\}]=G^{-1}(\rho)\overline{F}(G^{-1}(\rho))(1+o(1)).

Taking logarithms and using H⁡(s¯ρ)=−log⁡(1−ρ)H(\bar{s}_{\rho})=-\log(1-\rho) yields

H⁡(s¯ρ)=H⁡(G−1​(ρ))−log⁡G−1​(ρ)+log⁡𝔼⁡[S]+o⁡(1).H(\bar{s}_{\rho})=H(G^{-1}(\rho))-\log G^{-1}(\rho)+\log\mathbb{E}[S]+o(1).

The first condition of Assumption 1 gives log⁡G−1​(ρ)/H⁡(G−1​(ρ))→0\log G^{-1}(\rho)/H(G^{-1}(\rho))\to 0 and, by Lemma A.1, 𝔼⁡[S]\mathbb{E}[S] is finite. Dividing by H​(G−1​(ρ))H(G^{-1}(\rho)) proves the hazard-ratio limit. ∎

Lemma E.6 (Feasible proportional triggers).

Fix θ∈(0,θ¯)\theta\in(0,\bar{\theta}). For every fixed a∈[0,θ¯−θ)a\in[0,\bar{\theta}-\theta), the pair (θ,a​G−1​(ρ))(\theta,aG^{-1}(\rho)) is feasible for all sufficiently high loads. If HH is rapidly varying or regularly varying with positive index, then θ¯=1\bar{\theta}=1.

Proof of Lemma E.6.

Recall that τ¯ρ​(θ)=s¯ρ−θ​G−1​(ρ)\bar{\tau}_{\rho}(\theta)=\bar{s}_{\rho}-\theta G^{-1}(\rho). Lemma 3.4 gives

τ¯ρ​(θ)G−1​(ρ)=s¯ρG−1​(ρ)−θ⟶θ¯−θ.\frac{\bar{\tau}_{\rho}(\theta)}{G^{-1}(\rho)}=\frac{\bar{s}_{\rho}}{G^{-1}(\rho)}-\theta\longrightarrow\bar{\theta}-\theta.

Thus, for each fixed a∈[0,θ¯−θ)a\in[0,\bar{\theta}-\theta), we have 0≤a​G−1​(ρ)≤τ¯ρ​(θ)0\leq aG^{-1}(\rho)\leq\bar{\tau}_{\rho}(\theta) at all sufficiently high loads. This proves feasibility of the stated pair.

For the last claim, suppose θ¯<1\bar{\theta}<1 and choose a fixed c∈(θ¯,1)c\in(\bar{\theta},1). Lemma 3.4 gives s¯ρ<c​G−1​(ρ)\bar{s}_{\rho}<cG^{-1}(\rho) eventually. By monotonicity,

H⁡(s¯ρ)H​(G−1​(ρ))≤H⁡(c​G−1​(ρ))H​(G−1​(ρ)).\frac{H(\bar{s}_{\rho})}{H(G^{-1}(\rho))}\leq\frac{H(cG^{-1}(\rho))}{H(G^{-1}(\rho))}.

The left-hand side tends to 11 by Lemma E.5. The right-hand side tends to 00 under rapid variation, or to cν<1c^{\nu}<1 under regular variation with index ν>0\nu>0. Both contradict the inequality, so θ¯=1\bar{\theta}=1. ∎

E.4 Polylogarithmic Cumulative Hazards

Proposition E.7 (Trigger choice for polylogarithmic hazards).

Suppose H⁡(x)∼A​(log⁡x)mH(x)\sim A(\log x)^{m}, with A>0A>0 and m≥2m\geq 2, including lognormal-type tails at m=2m=2. Arrival queries make SPD eventually unstable, whereas the latest feasible trigger and every fixed proportional trigger a​G−1​(ρ)aG^{-1}(\rho), 0<a<θ¯−θ0<a<\bar{\theta}-\theta, give eventual stability and heavy-traffic order-optimality.

Proof of Proposition E.7.

For each stated trigger choice, Lemma E.6 gives feasibility at all sufficiently high loads. For every fixed t>0t>0, the polylogarithmic asymptotic and Lemma E.5 give

H⁡(t​G−1​(ρ))H⁡(s¯ρ)=H⁡(t​G−1​(ρ))H​(G−1​(ρ))​H​(G−1​(ρ))H⁡(s¯ρ)⟶1.\frac{H(tG^{-1}(\rho))}{H(\bar{s}_{\rho})}=\frac{H(tG^{-1}(\rho))}{H(G^{-1}(\rho))}\frac{H(G^{-1}(\rho))}{H(\bar{s}_{\rho})}\longrightarrow 1.

Recall from Section 5.1 that, for a feasible pair (θ,τ)(\theta,\tau), the self-information is Iρ​(θ,τ)=H⁡(τ+bρ​(θ))−H⁡(τ)I_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=H(\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta))-H(\tau). We use the preceding limit to evaluate Iρ​(θ,τ)/H⁡(s¯ρ)I_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)/H(\bar{s}_{\rho}) at each trigger and apply Lemma 5.3.

At-arrival queries. Since H⁡(0)=0H(0)=0, the definition of self-information gives

Positive proportional triggers. For every fixed a∈(0,θ¯−θ)a\in(0,\bar{\theta}-\theta), both aa and a+θa+\theta are positive. Substituting τ=a​G−1​(ρ)\tau=aG^{-1}(\rho) into the definition of self-information yields

pρqry​(θ,a2​G−1​(ρ))pρqry​(θ,a1​G−1​(ρ))\displaystyle\frac{p_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta,a_{2}G^{-1}(\rho))}{p_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}(\theta,a_{1}G^{-1}(\rho))} =exp⁡(Iρ​(θ,a2​G−1​(ρ))−Iρ​(θ,a1​G−1​(ρ)))\displaystyle=\exp\!\left(I_{\rho}(\theta,a_{2}G^{-1}(\rho))-I_{\rho}(\theta,a_{1}G^{-1}(\rho))\right) (16)

For 0<ν<10<\nu<1, strict concavity of xνx^{\nu} makes Ψν,θ\Psi_{\nu,\theta} strictly decreasing, so the exponent tends to −∞-\infty and the ratio tends to zero. At ν=1\nu=1, all fixed proportional triggers preserve slack if θ<γ\theta<\gamma, and all are unstable if θ>γ\theta>\gamma. Whenever Ψν,θ​(a)=γ\Psi_{\nu,\theta}(a)=\gamma, the finer terms in the relative inference load identity (9) determine the inference load. ∎

Appendix F Proofs for Inexact Predictions

We use the prediction rules and multiplicative error bound from Section 5. Appendix F.1 shows why the parameters used for exact predictions can fail with prediction error. Appendix F.2 states a response-time bound in terms of demoted work and applies it to the repair at arrival. Appendix F.3 then uses the same bound to give the detailed proof of Lemma 5.5. Finally, Appendix F.4 proves the response-time bound.

F.1 Failure of the Unadjusted Demotion Test

Recall from Section 4.2 the residual barrier and (θ,τ)(\theta,\tau)-tuned query probability

bρ​(θ)=θ​G−1​(ρ),qρ​(θ,τ)=1−ρF¯​(τ+bρ​(θ)).b_{\rho}(\theta)=\theta G^{-1}(\rho),\qquad q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau)=\frac{1-\rho}{\overline{F}(\tau+b_{\rho}(\theta))}.

A trigger is feasible when 0≤τ≤τ¯ρ​(θ)=s¯ρ−bρ​(θ)0\leq\tau\leq\bar{\tau}_{\rho}(\theta)=\bar{s}_{\rho}-b_{\rho}(\theta).

Proposition F.1 (Failure of the unadjusted demotion test).

For every fixed θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1) and ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), there exists a service distribution in the lognormal-or-lighter regime and an ε\varepsilon-inexact prediction rule such that, with free predictions, SPD⁡(bρ​(θ),qρ​(θ,τρ),τρ)\mathrm{SPD}(b_{\rho}(\theta),q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau_{\rho}),\tau_{\rho}) is not heavy-traffic order-optimal for any feasible deterministic trigger τρ\tau_{\rho}.

Proof.

We consider mean-one exponential service times and predictions that consistently underestimate size as much as the error model allows: S^=(1−ε)​S\widehat{S}=(1-\varepsilon)S. With the parameters in the proposition, SPD⁡(bρ​(θ),qρ​(θ,τρ),τρ)\mathrm{SPD}(b_{\rho}(\theta),q_{\rho}(\theta,\tau_{\rho}),\tau_{\rho}) demotes a queried job only when S>(τρ+bρ​(θ))/(1−ε)S>(\tau_{\rho}+b_{\rho}(\theta))/(1-\varepsilon). Write b=bρ​(θ)=θ​G−1​(ρ)b=b_{\rho}(\theta)=\theta G^{-1}(\rho). For mean-one exponential service, λρ=ρ\lambda_{\rho}=\rho, 1−ρ=(G−1​(ρ)+1)​e−G−1​(ρ)1-\rho=(G^{-1}(\rho)+1)e^{-G^{-1}(\rho)}, and s¯ρ=−log⁡(1−ρ)=G−1​(ρ)−log⁡(G−1​(ρ)+1)\bar{s}_{\rho}=-\log(1-\rho)=G^{-1}(\rho)-\log(G^{-1}(\rho)+1). Feasibility gives b≤τρ+b≤s¯ρ<G−1​(ρ)b\leq\tau_{\rho}+b\leq\bar{s}_{\rho}<G^{-1}(\rho), while the (θ,τρ)(\theta,\tau_{\rho})-tuned query probability is qρ​(θ,τρ)=(1−ρ)​eτρ+bq_{\rho}(\theta,\tau_{\rho})=(1-\rho)e^{\tau_{\rho}+b}. With QQ the independent sampling coin, the demotion indicator is R=Q𝟏{S>(τρ+b)/(1−ε)}R=Q\mathbf{1}\{S>(\tau_{\rho}+b)/(1-\varepsilon)\}. Direct integration of the exponential tail gives

𝔼⁡[(S−τρ)​R]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(S-\tau_{\rho})R] =(1−ρ)(τρ+b1−ε−τρ+1)e−ε(τρ+b)/(1−ε)\displaystyle=(1-\rho)\left(\frac{\tau_{\rho}+b}{1-\varepsilon}-\tau_{\rho}+1\right)e^{-\varepsilon(\tau_{\rho}+b)/(1-\varepsilon)}
≤(1−ρ)(G−1​(ρ)1−ε+1)e−εb/(1−ε)=o(1−ρ).\displaystyle\leq(1-\rho)\left(\frac{G^{-1}(\rho)}{1-\varepsilon}+1\right)e^{-\varepsilon b/(1-\varepsilon)}=o(1-\rho).

The upper bound does not depend on the feasible trigger. This higher threshold makes the expected work removed from high priority o⁡(1−ρ)o(1-\rho), uniformly over feasible triggers. 𝔼⁡[(S−(S−τρ)​R)2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(S-(S-\tau_{\rho})R)^{2}] ≥𝔼[S2{S≤b1−ε}]⟶𝔼[S2]=2.\displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}\!\left[S^{2}\mathbf{1}\!\left\{S\leq\frac{b}{1-\varepsilon}\right\}\right]\longrightarrow\mathbb{E}[S^{2}]=2.

F.2 Repair at Arrival

The following bound combines the two SOAP identities in Lemmas E.1 and E.2. It translates lower bounds on the fraction of jobs demoted and their remaining service into an upper bound on mean response time. We use it below for the repair at arrival and in Appendix F.3 for the delayed candidates. Its proof is deferred to Appendix F.4.

Lemma F.2 (Response time from demoted work).

At load 0<ρ<10<\rho<1, consider an SPD policy π\pi with free predictions, a deterministic trigger τ≥0\tau\geq 0, and FCFS in both queues with a prediction rule as defined in Section 5. Let RR indicate eventual demotion. If ℙ⁡(R=1)≥1−ρ\mathbb{P}(R=1)\geq 1-\rho and S−τ≥m>0S-\tau\geq m>0 whenever R=1R=1, then

𝔼⁡[Tπ]≤𝔼⁡[S2](1−ρ)​m+𝔼⁡[S]+1λ+τλ​m.\mathbb{E}[T^{\pi}]\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}[S^{2}]}{(1-\rho)m}+\mathbb{E}[S]+\frac{1}{\lambda}+\frac{\tau}{\lambda m}.

At τ=0\tau=0, we can account for the worst allowed underprediction by lowering the residual demotion barrier to (1−ε)​bρ​(θ)(1-\varepsilon)b_{\rho}(\theta), while keeping the θ\theta-tuned query probability qρ​(θ)q_{\rho}(\theta).

Proposition F.3 (Robustness with free predictions).

Suppose the service distribution is in the lognormal-or-lighter regime. For fixed θ∈(0,θ¯)\theta\in(0,\bar{\theta}) and ε∈[0,1)\varepsilon\in[0,1), the pair (θ,0)(\theta,0) is feasible for all sufficiently high loads. Under free ε\varepsilon-inexact predictions the policy

SPD⁡((1−ε)​bρ​(θ),qρ​(θ),0)\mathrm{SPD}\bigl((1-\varepsilon)b_{\rho}(\theta),q_{\rho}(\theta),0\bigr)

is heavy-traffic order-optimal, uniformly over the allowed prediction rules.

Proof.

Lemma 4.2 gives qρ​(θ)→0q_{\rho}(\theta)\to 0, so the pair (θ,0)(\theta,0) is feasible for all sufficiently high loads. Every queried job with S>bρ​(θ)S>b_{\rho}(\theta) is demoted, since S^≥(1−ε)​S>(1−ε)​bρ​(θ)\widehat{S}\geq(1-\varepsilon)S>(1-\varepsilon)b_{\rho}(\theta). Conversely, a demoted job satisfies (1+ε)​S≥S^>(1−ε)​bρ​(θ)(1+\varepsilon)S\geq\widehat{S}>(1-\varepsilon)b_{\rho}(\theta), so its size exceeds 1−ε1+ε​bρ​(θ)\frac{1-\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon}b_{\rho}(\theta). If pρdemp_{\rho}^{\mathrm{dem}} denotes the demoted fraction, independent sampling gives pρdem≥qρ​(θ)​F¯​(bρ​(θ))=1−ρp_{\rho}^{\mathrm{dem}}\geq q_{\rho}(\theta)\overline{F}(b_{\rho}(\theta))=1-\rho, and high-priority slack is at least λρ​1−ε1+ε​pρdem​bρ​(θ)\lambda_{\rho}\frac{1-\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon}p_{\rho}^{\mathrm{dem}}b_{\rho}(\theta).

Applying Lemma F.2 with τ=0\tau=0 and m=1−ε1+ε​bρ​(θ)m=\frac{1-\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon}b_{\rho}(\theta), we obtain 𝔼⁡[T]=O⁡(1/((1−ρ)​bρ​(θ))+1)\mathbb{E}[T]=O(1/((1-\rho)b_{\rho}(\theta))+1), uniformly over the allowed prediction rules. Since bρ​(θ)=θ​G−1​(ρ)b_{\rho}(\theta)=\theta G^{-1}(\rho), this gives the required heavy-traffic upper bound. SRPT optimality gives 𝔼⁡[T]≥𝔼⁡[TSRPT]\mathbb{E}[T]\geq\mathbb{E}[T^{\mathrm{SRPT}}] for every allowed prediction rule. The SRPT heavy-traffic characterization (2) supplies the matching lower bound. ∎

Appendix G Proofs for SRPT in the Low-Priority Queue (Section 4.3)

Appendix G.1 decomposes the chosen policy’s mean response time into the contributions of never-demoted jobs, demoted waiting, and demoted residence. Appendix G.2 uses bounds on these three contributions to prove heavy-traffic order-optimality with inference costs (Theorem G.1), recovering Theorem 4.7 when predictions are free. Appendix G.3 proves the three supporting lemmas.

G.1 The SOAP Identity for the Chosen Policy

With FCFS in both queues, ranks only increase at demotion, so there is no recycled relevant work. With an SRPT background, a demoted job’s rank rises at demotion and then decreases with its remaining service. An old job that crosses above a fixed rank threshold can therefore later cross back below it, creating a recycled relevant-work interval. The demoted tagged job’s worst future rank also changes during service. We therefore derive both the relevant-work terms and the residence integral explicitly below.

Consider SPD⁡(τρ,1,τρ,SRPT)\mathrm{SPD}(\tau_{\rho},1,\tau_{\rho},\mathrm{SRPT}) with τρ>0\tau_{\rho}>0: query when S>τρS>\tau_{\rho}, and demote when S>2​τρS>2\tau_{\rho}. For ease of presentation, we refer to this policy as SRPT​-​low\mathrm{SRPT\text{-}low}. Each query requires δρ≥0\delta_{\rho}\geq 0 units of server work, performed at high priority before any demotion; δρ=0\delta_{\rho}=0 is the case of free predictions. We write TSRPT​-​low​(δρ)T^{\mathrm{SRPT\text{-}low}}(\delta_{\rho}) for response time including inference. A demoted job receives τρ+δρ\tau_{\rho}+\delta_{\rho} units at high priority, then enters low priority with S−τρS-\tau_{\rho} ordinary service remaining. Assume

ρ⁡(δρ)=ρ+λρ​δρ​F¯​(τρ)<1.\rho(\delta_{\rho})=\rho+\lambda_{\rho}\delta_{\rho}\overline{F}(\tau_{\rho})<1.

High priority has rank zero, and the low-priority rank is the true remaining service. A new job of size S>sS>s can interrupt a demoted tagged job of size ss while receiving high-priority service and inference. At demotion, however, the new job has S−τρ>s−τρS-\tau_{\rho}>s-\tau_{\rho} service left, whereas the tagged job has at most s−τρs-\tau_{\rho} left. SRPT therefore gives the tagged job priority over this larger job until it completes. To apply Proposition B.2, we next compute the relevant-work terms for jobs already present when the tagged job arrives and for jobs that arrive afterward.

Relevant work and the SOAP denominators. The high-priority work and load of a generic arrival are

X0old[0]=S+δρ𝟏{S>τρ}−(S−τρ)𝟏{S>2τρ},ρHIGH(δρ)=λρ𝔼[X0old[0]].X_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[0]=S+\delta_{\rho}\mathbf{1}\{S>\tau_{\rho}\}-(S-\tau_{\rho})\mathbf{1}\{S>2\tau_{\rho}\},\qquad\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\delta_{\rho})=\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[X_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[0]].

For a demoted tagged job of size s>2​τρs>2\tau_{\rho}, the initial worst future rank is s−τρs-\tau_{\rho}. An old competitor starts at rank zero and is initially relevant. If S≤sS\leq s, its rank never exceeds s−τρs-\tau_{\rho}, so all its work remains relevant. If S>sS>s, it leaves relevance at demotion and reenters when its remaining service reaches s−τρs-\tau_{\rho}. Its original and recycled relevant intervals are therefore

X0old​[s−τρ]\displaystyle X_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[s-\tau_{\rho}] =(S+δρ𝟏{S>τρ})𝟏{S≤s}+(τρ+δρ)𝟏{S>s},\displaystyle=(S+\delta_{\rho}\mathbf{1}\{S>\tau_{\rho}\})\mathbf{1}\{S\leq s\}+(\tau_{\rho}+\delta_{\rho})\mathbf{1}\{S>s\},
X1old​[s−τρ]\displaystyle X_{1}^{\mathrm{old}}[s-\tau_{\rho}] =(s−τρ)𝟏{S>s},Xiold[s−τρ]=0(i≥2).\displaystyle=(s-\tau_{\rho})\mathbf{1}\{S>s\},\qquad X_{i}^{\mathrm{old}}[s-\tau_{\rho}]=0\quad(i\geq 2).

The second interval records a larger old job’s final s−τρs-\tau_{\rho} units, which it may already have reached before the tagged arrival. A new job cannot reach this interval ahead of the tag. Its original relevant work agrees with X0oldX_{0}^{\mathrm{old}} except at S=sS=s: old jobs win equal-rank FCFS ties and new jobs lose them. Since ties have probability zero (the service distribution has a density; see Section 2.1), ρ0old​[s−τρ]=ρnew​[s−τρ]\rho_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[s-\tau_{\rho}]=\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[s-\tau_{\rho}], and

1−ρnew[s−τρ]=1−ρ(δρ)+λρ𝔼[(S−τρ)𝟏{S>s}],s≥2τρ.1-\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[s-\tau_{\rho}]=1-\rho(\delta_{\rho})+\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[(S-\tau_{\rho})\mathbf{1}\{S>s\}],\qquad s\geq 2\tau_{\rho}. (17)

Here slack means this SOAP denominator factor: total-system slack plus the load excluded from new relevant work. At the smallest demotion rank, ρnew​[τρ]=ρHIGH​(δρ)\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[\tau_{\rho}]=\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\delta_{\rho}). By contrast, a never-demoted tag has rank zero throughout and ρnew​[0]=0\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[0]=0, since new arrivals lose its high-priority FCFS tie.

Residence follows the worst future rank. For a demoted tag of size s>2​τρs>2\tau_{\rho}, let aa count attained server work, including inference. Its total work is s+δρs+\delta_{\rho}, and its worst future rank is

r⁡(a)={s−τρ,0≤a≤τρ+δρ,s+δρ−a,τρ+δρ<a<s+δρ.r(a)=\begin{cases}s-\tau_{\rho},&0\leq a\leq\tau_{\rho}+\delta_{\rho},\\ s+\delta_{\rho}-a,&\tau_{\rho}+\delta_{\rho}<a<s+\delta_{\rho}.\end{cases}

The response-time decomposition. A never-demoted tag sees only older high-priority work and then its own service. For a demoted tag, the equal old/new loads give the squared waiting denominator below. Averaging the residence integral over tagged sizes replaces its upper limit by the weight ℙ​(S>u)=F¯​(u)\mathbb{P}(S>u)=\overline{F}(u). We group the response-time identity into never-demoted response time, demoted waiting, and demoted residence. Proposition B.2 gives

𝔼⁡[TSRPT​-​low​(δρ)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[T^{\mathrm{SRPT\text{-}low}}(\delta_{\rho})] =F(2τρ)λρ​𝔼​[(X0old​[0])2]2​(1−ρHIGH​(δρ))+𝔼[(S+δρ𝟏{S>τρ})𝟏{S≤2τρ}]⏟never-demoted jobs: Lemma G.2\displaystyle={}\underbrace{F(2\tau_{\rho})\frac{\lambda_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[(X_{0}^{\mathrm{old}}[0])^{2}]}{2(1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\delta_{\rho}))}+\mathbb{E}[(S+\delta_{\rho}\mathbf{1}\{S>\tau_{\rho}\})\mathbf{1}\{S\leq 2\tau_{\rho}\}]}_{\text{never-demoted jobs: Lemma~\ref{lem:sparse-srpt-high-negligible}}} (18)

The other two groups concern only demoted jobs, S>2​τρS>2\tau_{\rho}: the second is their SOAP waiting, and the third is their full SOAP residence. Its three terms follow the same order as the conditional residence formula above: the initial service and inference block, remaining service above τρ\tau_{\rho}, and the final τρ\tau_{\rho} units.

G.2 The SRPT Response-Time Bound

We prove the following extension of Theorem 4.7 to the inference-cost model of Section 5.

Theorem G.1 (Order-optimality with full-size predictions and inference costs).

Suppose the service distribution is in the intermediate regime or satisfies H⁡(x)∼A​(log⁡x)mH(x)\sim A(\log x)^{m}, with A>0A>0 and m≥2m\geq 2. Fix γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1) and β∈(1−γ,1)\beta\in(1-\gamma,1). Use exact full-size predictions with 0≤δρ≤(1−ρ)γ/λρ0\leq\delta_{\rho}\leq(1-\rho)^{\gamma}/\lambda_{\rho}, and set

τρ=F¯−1​((1−ρ)β),bρ=τρ,qρ=1.\tau_{\rho}=\overline{F}^{-1}\!\left((1-\rho)^{\beta}\right),\qquad b_{\rho}=\tau_{\rho},\qquad q_{\rho}=1.

Then SPD⁡(bρ,qρ,τρ,SRPT)\mathrm{SPD}(b_{\rho},q_{\rho},\tau_{\rho},\mathrm{SRPT}) is eventually stable and heavy-traffic order-optimal, with ex-ante query probability (1−ρ)β→0(1-\rho)^{\beta}\to 0.

For any β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), choosing γ∈(1−β,1)\gamma\in(1-\beta,1) and setting δρ=0\delta_{\rho}=0 recovers Theorem 4.7. We use the tuning above throughout the proof. The three lemmas bound the three groups in (18), in order: never-demoted jobs contribute negligibly, while demoted waiting and demoted residence are each bounded at the SRPT order. We state these facts first, prove the theorem from them, and give their proofs in Appendix G.3. All bounds are for sufficiently high load, with constants independent of ρ\rho; setting δρ=0\delta_{\rho}=0 also gives the free-prediction case.

Both regimes in the theorem satisfy H⁡(2​x)/H⁡(x)→1H(2x)/H(x)\to 1, the tail ratio used below. For a polylogarithmic cumulative hazard, H⁡(x)∼A​(log⁡x)mH(x)\sim A(\log x)^{m} with A>0A>0 and m≥2m\geq 2, so

H⁡(2​x)H⁡(x)=(1+o⁡(1))​(log⁡(2​x)log⁡x)m⟶1.\frac{H(2x)}{H(x)}=(1+o(1))\left(\frac{\log(2x)}{\log x}\right)^{m}\longrightarrow 1.

In the intermediate regime, Lemma A.2 gives h⁡(x)=o⁡(log⁡x/x)h(x)=o(\log x/x), and hence

H⁡(2​x)−H⁡(x)=∫x2​xh⁡(u)​𝑑u=o⁡(log⁡x)=o⁡(H⁡(x)).H(2x)-H(x)=\int_{x}^{2x}h(u)\,du=o(\log x)=o(H(x)).

The tuning also gives

pρqry=F¯​(τρ)=(1−ρ)β⟶0,λρ​δρ​pρqry≤(1−ρ)β+γ=o⁡(1−ρ).p_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}=\overline{F}(\tau_{\rho})=(1-\rho)^{\beta}\longrightarrow 0,\qquad\lambda_{\rho}\delta_{\rho}p_{\rho}^{\mathrm{qry}}\leq(1-\rho)^{\beta+\gamma}=o(1-\rho).

Hence 1−ρ⁡(δρ)∼1−ρ1-\rho(\delta_{\rho})\sim 1-\rho, so the policy is eventually stable and retains at least half the ordinary-service slack. Also τρ→∞\tau_{\rho}\to\infty and δρ→0\delta_{\rho}\to 0, giving δρ≤τρ\delta_{\rho}\leq\tau_{\rho} eventually.

Lemma G.2 (Response time of never-demoted jobs).

Jobs that finish at high priority contribute at most

𝔼[TSRPT​-​low(δρ)𝟏{S≤2τρ}]≤Cτρ​F¯​(2​τρ)+C=o(𝔼[TSRPT]).\mathbb{E}[T^{\mathrm{SRPT\text{-}low}}(\delta_{\rho})\mathbf{1}\{S\leq 2\tau_{\rho}\}]\leq\frac{C}{\tau_{\rho}\overline{F}(2\tau_{\rho})}+C=o\!\left(\mathbb{E}[T^{\mathrm{SRPT}}]\right).

The choice β<1\beta<1 sends enough work to low priority to make the response-time contribution of never-demoted jobs negligible.

Lemma G.3 (Waiting of demoted jobs).

The SOAP waiting contribution of demoted jobs satisfies

∫2​τρ∞λρ​∑i=01𝔼⁡[(Xiold​[s−τρ])2]2​(1−ρnew​[s−τρ])2​f​(s)​𝑑s≤16​𝔼​[TSRPT].\int_{2\tau_{\rho}}^{\infty}\frac{\lambda_{\rho}\sum_{i=0}^{1}\mathbb{E}[(X_{i}^{\mathrm{old}}[s-\tau_{\rho}])^{2}]}{2(1-\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[s-\tau_{\rho}])^{2}}f(s)\,ds\leq 16\mathbb{E}[T^{\mathrm{SRPT}}].

A larger competitor retains at least half its size at demotion. Our policy therefore excludes at least half the large-job work excluded by ordinary SRPT, while its relevant-work second moments increase by only a constant factor.

Lemma G.4 (Residence of demoted jobs).

The full SOAP residence contribution of demoted jobs satisfies

(τρ+δρ)​∫2​τρ∞f⁡(s)1−ρnew​[s−τρ]​𝑑s+∫2​τρ∞F¯​(s)1−ρnew​[s−τρ]​𝑑s+τρ​F¯​(2​τρ)1−ρHIGH​(δρ)\displaystyle(\tau_{\rho}+\delta_{\rho})\int_{2\tau_{\rho}}^{\infty}\frac{f(s)}{1-\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[s-\tau_{\rho}]}\,ds+\int_{2\tau_{\rho}}^{\infty}\frac{\overline{F}(s)}{1-\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[s-\tau_{\rho}]}\,ds+\frac{\tau_{\rho}\overline{F}(2\tau_{\rho})}{1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\delta_{\rho})}
≤2​𝔼​[TSRPT]+O⁡(log⁡11−ρ).\displaystyle\leq 2\mathbb{E}[T^{\mathrm{SRPT}}]+O\!\left(\log\frac{1}{1-\rho}\right).

The initial block adds only a logarithmic cost, the middle term is at most twice ordinary SRPT’s residence contribution, and the final τρ\tau_{\rho} units add a bounded cost.

Proof of Theorem G.1.

The setup above gives eventual stability and a vanishing ex-ante query probability. Lemmas G.2–G.4 bound the three groups in the response-time identity (18), respectively, yielding

𝔼⁡[TSRPT​-​low​(δρ)]≤18​𝔼​[TSRPT]+o⁡(𝔼⁡[TSRPT]).\mathbb{E}[T^{\mathrm{SRPT\text{-}low}}(\delta_{\rho})]\leq 18\mathbb{E}[T^{\mathrm{SRPT}}]+o\!\left(\mathbb{E}[T^{\mathrm{SRPT}}]\right).

For the lower bound, replace inference intervals by idle time. This gives an ordinary-service schedule with the same completion times, whose mean response time is at least that of SRPT. The SRPT benchmark (2) now gives the claimed order. ∎

dd​s​ρnew​[s−τρ]=λρ​(s−τρ)​f​(s),for almost every ​s≥2​τρ.\frac{d}{ds}\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[s-\tau_{\rho}]=\lambda_{\rho}(s-\tau_{\rho})f(s),\qquad\text{for almost every }s\geq 2\tau_{\rho}.

The same density weights the tagged sizes. Since s−τρ≥τρs-\tau_{\rho}\geq\tau_{\rho}, changing from size to relevant load gives

(τρ+δρ)​∫2​τρ∞f⁡(s)1−ρnew​[s−τρ]​𝑑s\displaystyle(\tau_{\rho}+\delta_{\rho})\int_{2\tau_{\rho}}^{\infty}\frac{f(s)}{1-\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[s-\tau_{\rho}]}\,ds ≤τρ+δρλρ​τρ​∫2​τρ∞dd​s​ρnew​[s−τρ]1−ρnew​[s−τρ]​ds=τρ+δρλρ​τρ​log⁡1−ρHIGH​(δρ)1−ρ⁡(δρ).\displaystyle\leq\frac{\tau_{\rho}+\delta_{\rho}}{\lambda_{\rho}\tau_{\rho}}\int_{2\tau_{\rho}}^{\infty}\frac{\frac{d}{ds}\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[s-\tau_{\rho}]}{1-\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[s-\tau_{\rho}]}\,ds=\frac{\tau_{\rho}+\delta_{\rho}}{\lambda_{\rho}\tau_{\rho}}\log\frac{1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\delta_{\rho})}{1-\rho(\delta_{\rho})}.

At the lower endpoint, new arrivals contribute only high-priority work; as s→∞s\to\infty, all their work becomes relevant. These give the logarithm’s two endpoints. Since δρ≤τρ\delta_{\rho}\leq\tau_{\rho}, λρ=Θ⁡(1)\lambda_{\rho}=\Theta(1), and 1−ρ⁡(δρ)≥(1−ρ)/21-\rho(\delta_{\rho})\geq(1-\rho)/2, the prefactor is bounded and the logarithm is at most log⁡(2/(1−ρ))\log(2/(1-\rho)).

For the middle term, the denominator comparison in the proof of Lemma G.3 gives

∫2​τρ∞F¯​(s)1−ρnew​[s−τρ]​𝑑s≤2​∫0∞F¯​(s)1−ρ​G​(s)​𝑑s≤2​𝔼​[TSRPT].\int_{2\tau_{\rho}}^{\infty}\frac{\overline{F}(s)}{1-\rho^{\mathrm{new}}[s-\tau_{\rho}]}\,ds\leq 2\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\overline{F}(s)}{1-\rho G(s)}\,ds\leq 2\mathbb{E}[T^{\mathrm{SRPT}}].

The tail-probability weight is the same as in ordinary SRPT residence, so only the denominator comparison is needed.

For the final τρ\tau_{\rho} units of demoted jobs, the load bound 1−ρHIGH​(δρ)≥λρ​τρ​F¯​(2​τρ)1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\delta_{\rho})\geq\lambda_{\rho}\tau_{\rho}\overline{F}(2\tau_{\rho}), derived in the proof of Lemma G.2, gives

τρ​F¯​(2​τρ)1−ρHIGH​(δρ)≤1λρ=O⁡(1).\frac{\tau_{\rho}\overline{F}(2\tau_{\rho})}{1-\rho^{\mathrm{HIGH}}(\delta_{\rho})}\leq\frac{1}{\lambda_{\rho}}=O(1).

Adding the initial, middle, and final residence bounds proves the lemma. The SRPT estimate 𝔼⁡[TSRPT]=(1−ρ)−1+o⁡(1)\mathbb{E}[T^{\mathrm{SRPT}}]=(1-\rho)^{-1+o(1)}, established in the proof of Lemma G.2, also shows that the logarithmic overhead is negligible. ∎
